title: RAG Fundamentals: Retrieval Meets Generation
content: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pairs a language model with an external knowledge source so it can answer questions using information it was never trained on. Instead of relying only on what the model memorized during training, a RAG system retrieves relevant text chunks from a document store at query time and inserts them into the model's prompt as context. This course walks through the three core stages of a RAG pipeline: indexing (splitting source documents into chunks and storing them so they can be searched later), retrieval (given a user's question, finding the chunks most relevant to it), and generation (handing the retrieved chunks to the model along with the original question so it can produce a grounded answer). You'll learn why chunking strategy matters -- split documents at the wrong boundaries and you separate a question from its answer before the model even sees it -- and why 'stuffing everything into a huge context window' is not the same thing as RAG: a system with no retrieval step, just a large prompt, has no way to prioritize what's actually relevant, and costs far more in tokens. By the end of this course you'll be able to explain, in plain language, what problem RAG solves, what its three stages are, and one concrete failure mode that breaks the pipeline even when the underlying model is capable.

sections.heading: What problem this solves
sections.body: A language model's knowledge is frozen at training time and lives entirely inside its weights. That creates two problems the moment you want to use it on anything real: it doesn't know about your data (your company's return policy, last week's incident postmortem, a codebase that didn't exist when the model was trained), and even on topics it does know, it can state something confidently and wrongly with no way for you to check where the claim came from. Two tempting fixes don't actually work. Fine-tuning bakes new facts into the weights, but it's slow, expensive to redo every time the underlying data changes, and it still gives you no way to point at a source for any given answer. Just pasting your whole knowledge base into the prompt ("stuff it in the context window") seems simpler, but it doesn't scale past a small handful of documents, costs real money in tokens on every single call whether or not the content is relevant to the question asked, and -- as you'll see in "Where it breaks" below -- large models get measurably worse at using information buried in the middle of a long prompt. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is the practical middle path: keep the model's weights untouched, keep your knowledge base external and updatable, and at the moment of each question, retrieve only the small number of passages actually relevant to it and hand those to the model as context. The model still does the writing; it just isn't asked to write from memory alone.

sections.heading: How the pipeline actually works
sections.body: A RAG system has three distinct stages, and conflating them is the single most common source of confusion for people new to this. Indexing happens ahead of time, offline: your source documents (PDFs, wiki pages, support tickets, whatever) get split into chunks -- typically a few hundred tokens each -- and each chunk is run through an embedding model that turns it into a vector, a list of a few hundred to a few thousand floating-point numbers that captures the chunk's meaning geometrically. Chunks with similar meaning end up as nearby vectors in that space. Those vectors get stored in an index (a vector database, or even just an in-memory array for a small corpus) alongside the original chunk text. Retrieval happens live, per query: the user's question gets embedded with that same embedding model, and the index is searched for the chunks whose vectors are closest to the question's vector -- usually via cosine similarity -- returning the top handful ("top-k", commonly 3 to 10) candidate chunks. Generation is the final step: those retrieved chunks get assembled into a prompt alongside the original question -- something like "Using only the following passages, answer the question: [chunks] [question]" -- and handed to the language model, which writes the actual answer grounded in that supplied text rather than its own memorized weights. The mental model worth keeping: indexing is a librarian shelving books by subject, retrieval is pulling the three most relevant books off the shelf for a specific question, and generation is a researcher who's told to answer using only the books handed to them, not their own general knowledge.

sections.heading: Where it breaks
sections.body: Three failure modes account for most of the times a RAG system gives a wrong or unhelpful answer, and none of them are the model "being dumb" -- they're upstream problems in retrieval that generation can't recover from. Bad chunk boundaries are the most common: if a document gets split mechanically every N tokens with no regard for meaning, you can easily sever a fact from the sentence that qualifies it -- a chunk boundary that lands between "the refund window is 30 days" and "unless the item was purchased during the holiday sale, in which case it's 60" produces a chunk that's confidently wrong on its own. The fix is chunking that respects natural boundaries (paragraphs, sections) and often overlaps chunks slightly so a fact and its immediate context aren't split apart. Embedding similarity is not the same as relevance -- a chunk can be semantically close to a question's wording while being the wrong answer to what's actually being asked (a question about "return policy for electronics" can retrieve a chunk about "return policy for clothing" because the vector space clusters them as topically similar, even though the specific answer differs). This is why real systems often add a second, more precise re-ranking step after the initial vector-similarity retrieval rather than trusting embeddings alone. Finally, even with perfect retrieval, models exhibit a documented "lost in the middle" effect: they attend much more reliably to information at the very start or very end of a long prompt than to something buried in the middle of ten retrieved chunks -- which is a direct, measured argument for retrieving fewer, more relevant chunks rather than more, weaker ones.

sections.heading: A worked example
sections.body: Say your knowledge base is a company's internal policy documents, already chunked and indexed, and a support agent asks: "Can a customer return a laptop they bought 45 days ago?" At query time, that question is embedded into a vector. The retrieval step searches the index and returns its top three closest chunks by similarity: one stating "Standard returns are accepted within 30 days of purchase with proof of purchase," a second stating "Electronics purchased through the extended-warranty program may be returned within 90 days," and a third, less relevant chunk about the company's shipping carrier policy that happened to score just high enough to make the cut. The generation step receives all three chunks plus the original question, with an instruction to answer only from what's provided. A well-grounded answer says something like: "Under the standard policy, no -- the window is 30 days. However, if this laptop was purchased through the extended-warranty program, the return window extends to 90 days, so it's worth confirming which program applies before declining the return." Notice what happened: the model didn't have to guess or rely on memorized general knowledge about return policies -- it synthesized an answer strictly from the two relevant retrieved passages, correctly ignored the irrelevant shipping-carrier chunk instead of forcing it into the answer, and even surfaced the ambiguity (which program applies) rather than picking one silently. That's the actual value RAG delivers: not just an answer, but an answer traceable to specific source passages, with irrelevant retrieved noise correctly set aside.

sections.heading: What's next
sections.body: Everything above assumed chunking and retrieval just work correctly -- the next course in this track, on chunking strategies, is where you'll dig into exactly how to split documents so a chunk boundary doesn't sever a fact from its context, which is the single highest-leverage thing you can control in a RAG system's quality. After that, the evaluation course covers how teams actually measure whether a RAG system's retrieval and generation are working, rather than eyeballing a few outputs and hoping.

title: Chunking Strategies: Splitting Documents Without Losing Meaning
content: How you split source documents into chunks determines whether retrieval can ever find the right answer, no matter how good your search algorithm is. This course compares fixed-size chunking (splitting every N characters or tokens, fast but blind to sentence and paragraph boundaries), recursive character splitting (trying paragraph breaks first, then sentences, then words, so chunks stay semantically coherent), and semantic chunking (using embedding similarity to find natural topic breaks). You'll learn the classic tradeoff: chunks that are too small lose surrounding context, so a retrieved sentence like 'it costs $49 per month' becomes useless without knowing what 'it' refers to; chunks that are too large dilute the embedding, mixing several topics into one vector so the chunk stops matching any single query well and wastes tokens on irrelevant text. You'll also learn why most production systems add overlap (for example a 50-100 token overlap between consecutive chunks) so that a fact sitting right at a boundary still appears intact in at least one chunk.

sections.heading: Fixed-Size Chunking: Fast, Blind, and Occasionally Cruel
sections.body: The simplest chunking strategy is also the most naive: pick a size -- say 500 characters or 256 tokens -- and cut the document every N units, regardless of what's actually at that boundary. It requires no understanding of the text, runs in linear time even over millions of documents, and is trivial to implement with a single loop over the token stream. The cost of that speed is that the splitter has no idea it's a splitter -- it will cut a sentence in half, sever a bullet point from its heading, or slice a table row away from its header row without hesitation. A chunk might end mid-clause with 'the refund policy applies only when the customer has,' and the next chunk picks up with 'not already redeemed a promotional credit.' Neither half means much alone. Fixed-size chunking is still useful for homogeneous, low-structure text like raw log files or transcripts where paragraph boundaries carry little semantic weight, but for structured documents -- manuals, contracts, wikis -- it's usually the first thing teams replace once retrieval quality becomes a priority.

sections.heading: Recursive Character Splitting: Respecting the Document's Own Structure
sections.body: Recursive character splitting fixes the blindness of fixed-size chunking by trying a prioritized list of separators before giving up and cutting arbitrarily. A typical implementation attempts to split on double newlines first (paragraph breaks), and only if a resulting piece still exceeds the target chunk size does it recurse into that piece and try the next separator down the list: single newlines, then sentence-ending punctuation like '. ' or '? ', then spaces, and only as a last resort an arbitrary character cut. This means a 280-token paragraph stays intact as one chunk even if the target size is 300 tokens, while a 900-token paragraph gets recursively broken at sentence boundaries rather than mid-word. LangChain's RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter and LlamaIndex's SentenceSplitter both work this way, and it's the default choice for the large majority of production RAG systems because it's still fast (no model inference required) but produces chunks that read as coherent units to a human, which usually also means they embed more coherently.

sections.heading: Semantic Chunking: Letting Embeddings Find the Seams
sections.body: Semantic chunking replaces character-count heuristics with a similarity signal: split the document into candidate units (often sentences), embed each one, and measure the cosine similarity between consecutive embeddings. Where similarity drops sharply -- say from 0.85 down to 0.4 -- that's treated as a topic boundary and a chunk break is inserted there, regardless of whether that lands at 150 tokens or 600. The appeal is that chunk boundaries track actual topic shifts instead of an arbitrary size threshold, so a chunk about pricing doesn't get artificially truncated partway through and glued to the start of a section about support hours. The tradeoff is cost and unpredictability: every candidate unit needs an embedding call before you've even built your index, chunk sizes become variable and harder to reason about for downstream token budgets, and the similarity-drop threshold itself is a hyperparameter that needs tuning per corpus. Most teams reach for semantic chunking only after recursive splitting has been tried and still produces poor retrieval on a specific document type, such as long-form narrative text with few structural cues.

sections.heading: The Goldilocks Problem: Too Small Loses Context, Too Large Dilutes Meaning
sections.body: Chunk size sits on a tradeoff curve with failure modes on both ends. Make chunks too small -- a single sentence, say -- and you strip away the context needed to interpret what's retrieved: a chunk containing only 'it costs $49 per month' is useless to a user or an LLM if the preceding sentence establishing what 'it' refers to (the Pro plan? an add-on? a one-time setup fee?) was split into a different chunk entirely. The fact is present in the corpus but not usable at the point of retrieval. Make chunks too large -- several pages -- and the embedding model has to compress multiple unrelated topics into one fixed-length vector, diluting it so the chunk no longer matches any single query well; a query about refund windows might retrieve a giant chunk that also covers shipping, warranties, and account setup, wasting most of the LLM's context window on irrelevant text it now has to read past. There's no universal correct chunk size -- 200-500 tokens is a common starting range -- because the right answer depends on how self-contained individual facts are in your source material.

sections.heading: Overlap: The Safety Net for Facts Sitting on a Boundary
sections.body: Even a well-tuned splitter will occasionally cut through the middle of an important fact, because chunk boundaries are set by size or structure, not by where every individual fact happens to live. Consider a document split into 300-token chunks with zero overlap, where a key fact spans the last 20 tokens of one chunk and the first 30 tokens of the next: neither chunk alone contains the complete fact, so neither one is likely to be retrieved as a strong match, and even if one is retrieved, the LLM only sees half the story. Production systems address this by adding overlap between consecutive chunks -- commonly 50 to 100 tokens, roughly 15-30% of a typical chunk -- so that the tail of one chunk is repeated at the head of the next. That redundancy means a boundary-straddling fact still appears whole in at least one chunk, at the cost of modestly larger index size and a small amount of duplicate content the retriever might return twice for the same query.

title: Evaluating RAG Systems: Beyond 'Does the Answer Look Right?'
content: A RAG system can fail in the retriever, the generator, or both, and eyeballing final answers rarely tells you which. This course introduces the standard split between retrieval metrics and generation metrics. Retrieval metrics like precision (what fraction of retrieved chunks are actually relevant) and recall (what fraction of relevant chunks were retrieved) tell you whether the search step is working, independent of what the model does with the results. Generation metrics like faithfulness (does the answer only state things supported by the retrieved chunks) and answer relevance (does the answer actually address the question) tell you whether the model used good context well. You'll learn why a golden dataset of representative questions with known correct answers and known relevant source chunks is essential: without it you can't separate 'the retriever found the wrong document' from 'the retriever found the right document but the model ignored it.' You'll also see why automated frameworks (like RAGAS-style faithfulness scoring using an LLM judge) are useful for catching regressions at scale, but should be spot-checked against human judgment.

sections.heading: Why Wrong Answers Don't Tell You Where the System Broke
sections.body: When a RAG system returns a bad answer, the temptation is to read the answer, decide it's wrong, and start tweaking prompts. That instinct skips the diagnostic step that actually matters: a RAG pipeline has two independent components that can each fail on their own, and a bad final answer is consistent with several different underlying causes. The retriever might return zero relevant chunks (a retrieval failure), the retriever might return exactly the right chunks and the generator might ignore them in favor of its parametric knowledge (a generation failure), or both might fail simultaneously. Consider a query where your retrieval metrics show high recall -- the golden-relevant chunks were in fact surfaced in the top-k results -- but the answer is still wrong. High recall rules out 'the retriever missed the document' as an explanation. What remains is that the generator had good context available and still produced an unsupported or off-target answer, which points squarely at prompt construction, context window ordering, or the model's tendency to fall back on its own training data instead of the supplied chunks. Splitting metrics by stage turns 'the answer is wrong' from a dead end into an actionable diagnosis.

sections.heading: Retrieval Metrics: Precision, Recall, and Their Ranked Variants
sections.body: Precision@k asks: of the k chunks you retrieved, what fraction were actually relevant? Recall@k asks: of all relevant chunks that exist in the corpus for this query, what fraction did you retrieve? These pull in opposite directions -- retrieving more chunks (raising k) tends to raise recall while diluting precision, since you're pulling in more marginal or irrelevant material alongside the good stuff. Neither metric alone captures ranking quality: a system that buries the one relevant chunk at position 8 out of 10 has the same precision@10 as one that puts it first, but the generator is far more likely to use context near the top of the prompt. That's where rank-aware metrics come in. Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) scores based on the position of the first relevant result (1/rank), rewarding systems that surface relevance early. NDCG (Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain) generalizes this to graded relevance -- some chunks are highly relevant, others tangentially so -- and discounts contributions logarithmically by position. Hit rate, simpler still, just asks whether at least one relevant chunk appeared in the top-k at all. Computing any of these requires per-query relevance judgments: a human or careful process has to label, for each candidate chunk, whether it's actually relevant to that specific question.

sections.heading: Generation Metrics: Faithfulness and Answer Relevance
sections.body: Faithfulness measures whether every claim in the generated answer is actually supported by the retrieved context -- it says nothing about whether the answer is true in some absolute sense, only whether the model stayed within its supplied evidence. The standard computational approach, popularized by frameworks like RAGAS, decomposes the answer into individual atomic claims (e.g., splitting 'the drug reduces symptoms by 40% and was approved in 2019' into two separate statements) and then runs each claim through an entailment check against the retrieved chunks, typically using an LLM as a natural-language-inference judge: does this chunk entail, contradict, or say nothing about this claim? The faithfulness score is the fraction of claims that are entailed. Answer relevance is a distinct axis measuring whether the answer addresses the actual question asked, independent of faithfulness -- an answer can be perfectly faithful to the context while completely dodging what was asked. One common technique generates several hypothetical questions the answer would be a good response to, embeds them, and compares their similarity to the original query's embedding; low similarity signals the answer wandered off-topic even if every sentence in it is well-supported.

sections.heading: Building a Golden Dataset You Can Actually Diagnose With
sections.body: None of the metrics above compute themselves -- they require ground truth, and for RAG that ground truth has two layers most teams underestimate at first. First, for every query in your evaluation set, you need the known-relevant chunk IDs from your corpus, usually produced by a subject-matter expert reading candidate passages and labeling each as relevant, partially relevant, or irrelevant to that specific question. Second, you need a reference answer (or a rubric describing what a correct answer must contain) so generation metrics have something to check the output against. Without both layers you cannot decompose failures: retrieval metrics need the relevant-chunk labels, generation metrics need the reference answer, and you need both computed on the same queries to tell whether a bad answer came from bad retrieval or bad generation. Practically, a golden set of 50-200 queries is enough to start catching regressions, stratified across query types you actually see in production -- simple factual lookups, multi-hop questions requiring synthesis across chunks, and edge cases like questions with no good answer in the corpus at all, which test whether the system correctly declines to answer rather than hallucinating.

sections.heading: Automated LLM-Judge Scoring vs Human Spot-Checks
sections.body: Running an SME through hundreds of query-answer pairs by hand doesn't scale to a CI pipeline that needs to catch regressions on every prompt change or model swap. RAGAS-style frameworks address this by substituting a capable LLM as the judge for faithfulness, answer relevance, and similar metrics, which lets you score a full regression suite in minutes instead of days and rerun it on every pull request. But LLM judges carry known biases worth budgeting for: they tend toward self-preference (favoring outputs that resemble their own generation style), verbosity bias (rating longer answers as more thorough even when they aren't), and inconsistency near ambiguous entailment calls where a claim is 'mostly but not fully' supported. The practical fix isn't to distrust automation wholesale, it's to calibrate it: periodically pull a random sample -- 10-20 examples -- of the LLM judge's scores and have a human re-score the same examples blind, then compare. Large or systematic disagreement means the judge prompt needs revision or the metric isn't measuring what you think; agreement within a tolerance means you can trust the automated score between calibration checks.

title: Vector Databases: How Similarity Search Actually Works
content: Vector databases store embeddings (numeric representations of text meaning) and let you ask 'which stored vectors are closest to this query vector?' at scale. This course covers why exact nearest-neighbor search becomes too slow once you have millions of vectors, and how approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) algorithms like HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs) trade a small amount of accuracy for massive speed gains by building a graph structure that lets search skip most of the dataset. You'll learn why cosine similarity (or dot product on normalized vectors) is the standard distance metric for text embeddings, how embedding dimensionality (384, 768, 1536, etc.) affects both storage cost and retrieval quality, and why metadata filtering (restricting search to, say, documents from the last 30 days or a specific customer) needs to be combined carefully with vector search rather than applied as an afterthought. You'll also learn when a vector database is overkill: if your corpus is small or queries are mostly exact keyword lookups, a simpler full-text search index can outperform embeddings on both cost and accuracy.

sections.heading: Why Exact Nearest-Neighbor Search Collapses at Scale
sections.body: Brute-force k-NN computes the distance from a query vector to every stored vector -- O(n*d) per query. At 1 million vectors of 768 dimensions, that's roughly 768 million floating-point operations just to score candidates, before any sorting happens. At the 10-100 million vector scale typical of a production RAG corpus (millions of source documents chunked into a few hundred tokens each), exact search latency climbs into the hundreds of milliseconds to seconds per query, and it scales linearly -- doubling your corpus doubles your query time. ANN algorithms accept a small recall loss (often targeting 95-99% recall@10 instead of guaranteed 100%) in exchange for sublinear query time, frequently in the low single-digit milliseconds even across hundreds of millions of vectors. Production teams tune for a target recall rather than exactness, because the accuracy lost to approximation rarely changes which chunks actually end up in the LLM's context window.

sections.heading: Inside HNSW: Layered Graphs and Greedy Search That Skips Most of the Dataset
sections.body: HNSW organizes vectors into a multi-layer graph. Layer 0, the bottom, is dense: every vector is a node, connected to roughly M=16-64 of its approximate nearest neighbors. Each layer above contains an exponentially shrinking, probabilistically-chosen subset of those nodes -- similar to a skip list -- so layer 1 might hold a fraction of layer 0's nodes, layer 2 fewer still, up to a sparse top layer with only a handful of entry candidates. A search starts at a single entry point on the top layer and greedily hops to whichever neighbor is closer to the query, continuing until no neighbor improves the distance, then drops down one layer and repeats with a wider candidate list, until it bottoms out at layer 0. Because each layer roughly halves the effective search space and the graph's 'small world' property keeps any two nodes reachable in few hops, a query against 10 million vectors typically ends up comparing against only a few hundred to a few thousand candidates -- not all 10 million. That logarithmic-ish traversal is the entire mechanism behind HNSW's speed; the tradeoff is extra RAM to store the graph edges on top of the raw vectors, and non-trivial index build time.

sections.heading: Choosing a Distance Metric: Cosine, Dot Product, and Euclidean
sections.body: Text embedding models (OpenAI's text-embedding-3, Cohere embed, open models like BGE or E5) are trained so semantic similarity tracks the angle between vectors, not their magnitude. Cosine similarity measures that angle directly: (A*B)/(|A||B|), ranging from -1 to 1. If vectors are normalized to unit length at index time -- a cheap one-time step -- cosine similarity collapses to a plain dot product, which is cheaper to compute at query time since it skips the norm calculations. That's why most vector databases (pgvector, Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant) advertise 'cosine' as a metric option but actually normalize on ingestion and run dot product under the hood. Euclidean (L2) distance sees less use for text because embedding magnitude can drift with text length or model-specific artifacts unrelated to meaning, which skews raw distance; L2 stays standard for embedding spaces (some vision models) where magnitude itself is meaningful.

sections.heading: Embedding Dimensionality: The Storage-vs-Quality Tradeoff
sections.body: Dimensionality varies by model -- 384 for compact models like all-MiniLM, 768 for BERT-derived encoders, 1536 for OpenAI's text-embedding-3-small, up to 3072 for larger variants -- and it sets storage and compute cost directly. A single 1536-dim float32 vector is 6KB; 10 million such vectors is 60GB of raw vector data before graph overhead or replication. Higher dimensionality tends to capture more semantic nuance, but with diminishing returns: doubling dimensions rarely doubles recall, and past a point you're paying extra RAM, index-build time, and per-query compute for marginal quality gains. Techniques like scalar quantization (storing int8 instead of float32) and Matryoshka-trained embeddings (which stay useful when truncated to fewer dimensions) exist specifically to claw back that cost. Picking dimensionality is a real production tradeoff, not just 'use the biggest model' -- retrieval quality on typical RAG corpora often flattens out well before 1536 dimensions.

sections.heading: Metadata Filtering Done Right -- and When to Skip the Vector Database Entirely
sections.body: Metadata filtering restricts search to a subset -- customer_id = X, published within the last 30 days, doc_type = 'policy'. Bolted on naively as post-filtering (run vector search first, then discard non-matching results), it breaks silently: if the top-k nearest neighbors happen to belong to the wrong customer or are too old, filtering can return zero relevant results even though matching documents exist deeper in the ranked list. The opposite naive approach -- filter first, then brute-force the filtered subset -- throws away the ANN index's speed advantage entirely. Production systems instead push the predicate into the traversal itself (HNSW variants that skip non-matching nodes mid-search) or maintain separate sub-indexes per common filter value. Get this wrong and results look plausible while being quietly incomplete, a failure mode that's easy to miss since most queries still return something. And when the corpus is small (a few thousand documents) or queries are mostly exact lookups -- SKU numbers, ticket IDs, exact phrases -- a full-text index like BM25 or Postgres tsvector usually beats vector search on both cost and precision; embeddings win on fuzzy, semantic queries, not exact matches.

title: Agentic RAG: Retrieval as a Tool, Not a Fixed Pipeline Step
content: Classic RAG retrieves once, then generates once -- a fixed pipeline. Agentic RAG instead gives the model retrieval as a tool it can call repeatedly and reason about, which matters for multi-hop questions that no single retrieval pass can answer (for example, 'which of our vendors had the highest renewal cost increase compared to last year's contract?' requires finding two separate documents and comparing them). This course covers iterative retrieve-reason loops where the model decides whether it has enough evidence yet or needs to search again with a refined query, query decomposition (breaking a complex question into sub-questions that are each independently retrievable), and query rewriting (reformulating a vague user question into a more retrievable form before searching). You'll also learn about self-critique patterns, where the model checks its own draft answer against the retrieved evidence before finalizing, catching cases where it drifted from the sources. The core judgment call this course builds: recognizing when a question is genuinely multi-hop (static single-shot RAG will fail) versus when it just looks complex but is answerable from one good retrieval.

sections.heading: Why a Fixed Retrieve-Then-Generate Pipeline Breaks on Multi-Hop Questions
sections.body: Classic RAG embeds the user's question once, pulls the top-k chunks by vector similarity, stuffs them into the context window, and generates a single answer -- there is no mechanism for the model to say 'this isn't enough, let me look again.' That works fine when the answer lives in one chunk. It fails on questions like 'which of our vendors had the highest renewal cost increase compared to last year's contract?' because a single embedding of that whole question is semantically close to any document mentioning vendor renewals and costs -- a top-k=5 search will likely surface fragments of several vendors' current-year contracts (they're all lexically similar to the query) while missing prior-year contracts almost entirely, since 'last year' isn't a concept embeddings capture reliably. No single chunk contains both numbers for even one vendor, let alone the comparison across all of them. The judgment call this course builds: a question is genuinely multi-hop when answering it requires combining evidence that lives in separate documents at separate times or from separate entities -- comparisons, aggregations, or chained lookups. A question that merely sounds complex (e.g., 'what's included in Acme's support tier') but is fully answered by one well-chosen chunk is not multi-hop, and routing it through an expensive iterative loop just adds latency for no benefit.

sections.heading: The Iterative Retrieve-Reason Loop: A Worked Trace
sections.body: In agentic RAG, retrieval is exposed to the model as a callable tool inside its reasoning loop: generate a query, retrieve, inspect what came back, decide 'sufficient' or 'insufficient,' and if insufficient, issue a refined query. Trace the vendor question through three iterations. Iteration 1: the model doesn't yet know which vendors even have upcoming renewals, so it queries 'vendor renewal contracts 2026' and retrieves current-year renewal notices for Acme, Globex, and Initech -- three current costs, zero prior-year costs. Iteration 2: the model checks sufficiency, notices it can't compute an increase without a baseline, and queries 'Acme Globex Initech contract pricing 2025.' This retrieves last year's Acme and Globex contracts but misses Initech's, because that document is filed under 'Initech MSA renewal' rather than 'contract' -- a naming mismatch the query didn't anticipate. Iteration 3: the model notices the gap (two vendors have both years, one doesn't) and issues a targeted follow-up, 'Initech master service agreement 2025,' which fills it. Now every vendor has a symmetric before/after pair, the model computes deltas (say Acme +9%, Globex +22%, Initech +14%), and answers Globex. The stopping rule is coverage, not a fixed iteration count: loop while any entity the question implies lacks evidence at the same granularity as the others, and cap iterations (typically 4-6) so a persistently unfindable document produces an 'insufficient evidence' answer rather than an infinite search or a hallucinated number.

sections.heading: Query Decomposition: Splitting One Question Into Independently Retrievable Sub-Questions
sections.body: Query decomposition takes a complex question and, before retrieval starts, breaks it into sub-questions each answerable by its own single retrieval pass -- as opposed to the iterative loop, which discovers the need for a follow-up query reactively after seeing what came back. For the vendor question, a decomposition planner produces something like: (1) which vendors have a renewal in the current period, (2) what is each vendor's current renewal cost, (3) what was each vendor's cost in last year's contract, (4) compute percent increase per vendor, (5) select the maximum. Each sub-question maps to a retrieval query with a narrow, well-defined target, which tends to get better precision than one broad query trying to cover the whole comparison at once. The catch: decomposition assumes the planner already knows the shape of the data -- here, that there are exactly three vendors -- and it often doesn't until retrieval has run at least once. In practice the two patterns combine: an initial coarse decomposition ('find all vendors, then find pricing for each') gets revised mid-stream as the loop learns the actual vendor count, rather than committing to a rigid sub-question list upfront.

sections.heading: Query Rewriting: Turning a Vague User Question Into a Retrievable One
sections.body: Users don't phrase questions the way documents are written, and embedding the raw question often retrieves poorly -- query rewriting reformulates it into something closer to the target document's vocabulary before search runs. A user asking 'which vendor is being difficult right now' has nothing retrievable in it: no entity, no timeframe, no concrete subject. A rewrite might resolve it to 'vendor escalations open support tickets Q3 2026,' pulling in context (the current quarter, the domain-specific term 'escalations') the user didn't spell out. A related technique, HyDE (hypothetical document embeddings), sidesteps the mismatch differently: instead of embedding the question, the model first drafts a hypothetical answer in the style of the target documents and embeds that instead, because answer-shaped text sits closer in embedding space to real answer-shaped documents than question-shaped text does. Entity resolution matters too -- a user referencing 'the Acme deal' should be rewritten to the full entity name used in the corpus, 'Acme Corp master service agreement,' since sparse or hybrid retrieval will miss the informal alias entirely. Rewriting typically happens once, upfront, and decomposition (if needed) operates on the rewritten form rather than the user's original phrasing.

sections.heading: Self-Critique: Verifying a Draft Answer Against the Literal Retrieved Text
sections.body: Before finalizing, an agentic RAG system can have the model re-read its own draft answer against the retrieved chunks and check each claim for support, rather than trusting the generation pass to have stayed faithful to the sources. In the vendor example, the draft claims 'Globex increased 22%.' A real self-critique step re-derives that number by locating the exact spans it came from -- Globex's 2025 figure in one chunk, its 2026 figure in another -- and confirms both spans are actually attributed to Globex, not accidentally to Initech's chunk that happened to sit adjacent to it in a densely packed context window. This attribution slip is the most common failure mode when several similarly formatted contract chunks are retrieved together: the model computes a correct-looking percentage from the wrong pair of numbers. A weak self-critique prompt ('are you sure this is right?') tends to just rationalize the existing draft, since the model has no new information to reconsider. An effective one forces the model to quote the supporting span for every factual claim and treats any claim without a quotable span as a trigger to loop back into another retrieval round or to hedge the answer explicitly rather than present an unverified number as fact.

quiz.question: What distinguishes agentic RAG from classic single-shot RAG?
options: Agentic RAG never uses embeddings
The model can call retrieval repeatedly and decide whether it has enough evidence, rather than retrieving once and generating once
Agentic RAG is only for image data
There is no difference, just marketing

quiz.question: Why does a multi-hop question like comparing two vendor contracts challenge classic single-shot RAG?
options: It requires finding and combining evidence from separate retrieval steps that one search pass won't surface together
Multi-hop questions are always shorter than single-hop ones
Classic RAG can't handle numbers
