quiz.question: What is 'query decomposition' in an agentic RAG system?
options: Deleting the user's original query
Breaking a complex question into sub-questions that are each independently retrievable
Compressing the vector database
A method for fine-tuning the generator model

title: Hybrid Search and Reranking: When Embeddings Alone Aren't Enough
content: Dense embedding search is excellent at matching meaning but surprisingly weak at exact-match lookups: a query for a specific model number, error code, or product SKU can retrieve semantically 'close' but factually wrong chunks because embeddings compress away rare tokens. Hybrid search combines dense vector search with sparse keyword search (commonly BM25, a classic term-frequency ranking algorithm) and merges the two ranked lists, so exact terms still surface even when their embedding neighbors look similar. This course also covers reranking: after an initial retrieval step returns, say, the top 50 candidate chunks cheaply, a more expensive cross-encoder model rescoring the query against each candidate individually can reorder them far more accurately than the original similarity score, because a cross-encoder actually reads the query and chunk together rather than comparing pre-computed vectors. You'll learn the practical pattern: cheap broad retrieval first, expensive precise reranking second, applied only to a small candidate set to keep latency and cost reasonable.

sections.heading: Why Dense Embeddings Miss Exact Matches
sections.body: An embedding model is trained to compress a chunk of text into a few hundred to a few thousand floating-point numbers that capture its overall semantic gist -- topic, sentiment, intent. That compression is precisely what makes it bad at exact-match lookups. A query like 'error code E-4021' or 'model number WRX-350B' gets embedded into a vector that mostly encodes 'this is a technical error/model identifier,' and the rare alphanumeric token itself contributes only a small nudge to the final vector because the model has seen it few or zero times during training. The result: a chunk discussing a completely different error code, or no code at all, can sit closer in vector space than the chunk containing the literal exact string, simply because both chunks are 'about troubleshooting.' This isn't a bug you can fix by choosing a better embedding model -- it's structural. Any model that maps variable-length text to a fixed-size dense vector must throw away some information, and rare, high-specificity tokens (SKUs, part numbers, exact error strings, legal citations, drug names) are exactly the information most likely to get smoothed over in favor of broader thematic similarity.

sections.heading: Sparse Retrieval and BM25 as the Exact-Match Counterweight
sections.body: BM25 is the workhorse sparse-retrieval algorithm and the usual second leg of a hybrid system. Unlike dense embeddings, it never compresses the document into a fixed vector -- it keeps an inverted index mapping every literal term to the documents containing it, then scores a candidate by term frequency (how often the query term appears in this document) weighted inversely by how common that term is across the whole corpus, with length normalization so long documents don't win purely by repetition. A query for 'WRX-350B' matches BM25 almost perfectly: either the string is in the document or it isn't, and if it is, it dominates the score because that token is rare corpus-wide (high inverse document frequency). Hybrid search runs both retrievers over the same query and merges the two ranked lists, commonly with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (summing 1/(k + rank) for each document across both lists, k typically around 60) rather than trying to normalize and average two incomparable raw score scales. The dense side still contributes: it surfaces paraphrases and conceptually related chunks that share no literal tokens with the query, which BM25 alone would miss entirely.

sections.heading: The Two-Stage Funnel: Cheap Retrieval, Expensive Reranking
sections.body: Production RAG systems almost never run an expensive scoring model over the entire corpus -- that doesn't scale past a few thousand documents. Instead they use a funnel. Stage one is cheap and broad: hybrid dense-plus-BM25 retrieval (or dense alone) scans the full corpus, which might be millions of chunks, using approximate nearest-neighbor search and an inverted index, both of which are sub-linear and can return, say, the top 50 candidates in single-digit milliseconds. Stage two is expensive and narrow: a cross-encoder reranker rescores only those 50 candidates against the query, one pair at a time, and the results are cut down to the top 3-5 that actually get passed into the LLM's context window. The 50-to-5 ratio isn't arbitrary -- it reflects a bet that the cheap retriever's recall at 50 is high enough that the true best answers are almost always somewhere in that set, so the expensive model's job is purely to re-sort a small, already-relevant pool rather than to search. Widen the candidate set (say to 100 or 200) if you suspect stage-one recall is the bottleneck; narrow it (say to 20) if reranking latency is the bottleneck -- this ratio is the main dial you have for trading cost against recall.

sections.heading: Cross-Encoders vs. Bi-Encoders: Why Reranking Is More Accurate and Slower
sections.body: The embedding model used in stage-one retrieval is a bi-encoder: it encodes the query and each document independently into separate vectors, ahead of time for documents, and compares them with a cheap operation like cosine similarity. That independence is exactly what makes it fast -- document vectors are precomputed once at indexing time and reused for every future query, and comparing vectors at query time is just arithmetic. A cross-encoder reranker throws that independence away on purpose: it concatenates the query and a single candidate chunk into one input sequence and runs the whole thing through a transformer together, so every token of the query can attend to every token of the chunk (and vice versa) before producing a single relevance score. This lets it catch fine-grained interactions a bi-encoder structurally cannot see -- negation, exact term overlap, whether the chunk answers the specific question asked versus just being topically adjacent. The cost is that nothing about a cross-encoder score can be precomputed: each query-candidate pair requires its own full forward pass, which is why you only ever apply it to a small shortlist (tens of candidates) rather than an entire corpus of millions.

sections.heading: Tuning Hybrid Weights and Recognizing When Reranking Won't Save You
sections.body: Hybrid search isn't a fixed 50/50 blend -- the right balance between dense and sparse signal is domain-dependent and worth tuning deliberately. A legal or medical corpus full of precise terminology, citations, and codes should lean sparse-heavy; a corpus of casual support chat transcripts, where the same idea gets phrased a dozen different ways, should lean dense-heavy. Watch for a failure mode specific to Reciprocal Rank Fusion: it only sees rank position, not score magnitude, so a BM25 list that's mostly noise (near-zero real relevance) can still shove a garbage document into the top 5 purely by being first in that list -- rank-based fusion has no way to express 'this whole sparse result set is weak, discount it.' Reranking helps quality but does not fix a broken retrieval stage: if the true relevant chunk never makes it into the top-50 candidate set in the first place, a cross-encoder never gets the chance to find it, no matter how good it is at reordering the 50 it was handed. Debugging a bad final answer should always start by checking whether the answer was even in the candidate pool before blaming the reranker.

quiz.question: Why might a query for an exact product SKU fail with pure dense embedding search?
options: Embeddings compress away rare or exact tokens, so semantically 'close' but factually wrong chunks can outrank the exact match
Dense search cannot process numbers at all
SKUs are too long to embed
This never happens in practice

quiz.question: What is the typical two-stage pattern for combining retrieval and reranking?
options: Rerank first on the whole corpus, then retrieve
Cheap broad retrieval over the full corpus first, then expensive precise reranking on a small candidate set
Only ever use one stage
Reranking replaces retrieval entirely

quiz.question: Why is a cross-encoder reranker generally more accurate than the original similarity score, but also more expensive?
options: It reads the query and each candidate chunk together instead of comparing pre-computed vectors, which costs more compute per comparison
It uses a smaller model with fewer parameters
It skips the embedding step entirely for free
Cross-encoders are not actually more accurate

title: What Is an LLM, Really?
content: A large language model is, at its core, a statistical model trained to predict the next token given the tokens before it, learned from an enormous corpus of text. This course demystifies what that means in practice: the model has no database of facts it looks up, no memory of specific training documents it can cite, and no built-in notion of 'true' versus 'false' -- it has learned patterns of what text tends to follow other text, at a scale detailed enough that those patterns encode a remarkable amount of world knowledge and reasoning-like behavior. You'll learn why this framing explains both LLM strengths (fluent, context-sensitive generation across almost any topic) and their characteristic weaknesses (confident-sounding fabrication when the learned patterns don't actually contain the answer, sensitivity to how a question is phrased, and no reliable way to know what it doesn't know). Understanding an LLM as 'next-token prediction at scale' rather than as a search engine or a reasoning engine is the single most useful mental model for predicting when it will succeed and when it will quietly fail.

sections.heading: Next-Token Prediction: The One Mechanism Underneath Everything
sections.body: An LLM is trained on one objective: given a sequence of tokens (pieces of words, typically a few characters each, drawn from a vocabulary of 50,000-100,000 entries), predict a probability distribution over what token comes next. Training runs this over a corpus of trillions of tokens -- web pages, books, code, forum posts -- adjusting billions of internal weights via gradient descent so the model's predicted distribution gets closer to what actually followed in the real text. At generation time the model runs autoregressively: it predicts one token, appends it to the input, and repeats, one token at a time, each new token conditioned on everything before it including its own prior outputs. There is no separate 'thinking' phase and no lookup step -- every single token, whether it's finishing a sentence or stating a fact, comes out of the same forward pass through the same weights. A 'temperature' setting controls how much randomness is injected when sampling from that distribution, which is why the same prompt can produce different wording on different runs.

sections.heading: Where the Knowledge Lives: Compressed Weights, Not a Database
sections.body: When an LLM answers a factual question correctly, it isn't retrieving a stored record -- there is no row in a table that says 'capital of France = Paris' and no pointer back to the Wikipedia article it read during training. What training does is adjust weights (a 7-billion or 70-billion-parameter model has that many individually tuned numbers) so that, statistically, 'Paris' becomes the highest-probability continuation after tokens resembling 'The capital of France is'. That association got reinforced because the pattern appeared, in some form, thousands of times across the training corpus. This is why an LLM can't cite the specific document a fact came from, can't tell you whether a given fact appeared once or a million times, and can't distinguish 'I have overwhelming statistical support for this' from 'I have one and pattern-matched confidently anyway' -- the weights only encode the net effect of training, not a traceable provenance chain back to any source.

sections.heading: Confident Fabrication: Why Hallucination Isn't a Bug, It's the Mechanism
sections.body: Ask an LLM about a real historical event and a fabricated one phrased with the same confident structure, and it will often answer both the same way: fluently, specifically, and with no hedge. That's because the model has no separate fact-checking module that runs before it commits to an answer -- it is always doing the same thing, predicting the most plausible next tokens given the prompt, whether or not the training data actually contained the answer. If the patterns in the prompt statistically resemble the start of a citation, the model will complete a citation-shaped string, complete with a plausible-looking author, year, and journal, even when no such paper exists. This is 'confabulation' in the clinical sense: the output is generated by the same fluent process regardless of whether it's grounded in a real, frequently-reinforced pattern or a spurious one. Instruction-tuning and RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback) can nudge the model toward hedging or refusing on some known-uncertain categories of question, but that's a learned add-on layer on top of next-token prediction, not a change to the underlying mechanism -- so its coverage is uneven and easy to slip past with unfamiliar phrasing.

sections.heading: Why Rephrasing a Question Changes the Answer
sections.body: Because generation is conditioned on the exact sequence of tokens in the prompt, two questions that mean the same thing to a person can land in very different regions of the model's learned probability space if they're phrased differently -- different word choice, different tokenization, different order, extra qualifiers. A prompt worded like a homework question may pull toward the fluent, textbook-style completions that dominate the training data for that phrasing; the same underlying question worded like a casual Slack message may pull toward a shorter, hedgier, differently-sourced pattern of completions. This is why adding a single clarifying phrase, an example, or a system instruction ('answer step by step,' 'cite only what you're sure of') can measurably change output quality -- it's not the model 'understanding better,' it's the prompt tokens shifting which learned patterns dominate the next-token distribution. It also means there's no fixed, stable 'true answer' sitting inside the model waiting to be extracted correctly -- there's a distribution that phrasing steers.

sections.heading: Not a Search Engine, Not a Reasoning Engine: The Model That Actually Predicts Behavior
sections.body: Treating an LLM as a search engine implies it looks things up and can tell you when nothing was found; treating it as a reasoning engine implies a dedicated logic process checks each step for validity. Neither exists. What's underneath both the model's greatest strength and its most characteristic failure is the identical mechanism: next-token prediction learned from patterns at massive scale. Fluent, context-sensitive generation on almost any topic and confident-sounding fabrication when the topic outstrips what training reinforced are two outputs of that same process, not two different modes the model switches between. That's why 'next-token prediction at scale' outperforms the other two framings for predicting real behavior: it explains why the model is remarkably good at well-represented patterns (common code, common facts, common phrasing) and why it degrades ungracefully rather than gracefully on the long tail -- it doesn't know what it doesn't know, because 'knowing that you don't know' was never the objective it was trained on.

quiz.question: What is the most accurate description of what an LLM fundamentally does?
options: Looks up facts in an internal database
Predicts the next token given prior tokens, based on patterns learned from training text
Executes retrieval queries against the internet in real time
Runs a symbolic logic engine over the input

quiz.question: Why can an LLM produce confident-sounding but false statements?
options: It deliberately tries to deceive users
It generates plausible-sounding text based on learned patterns, with no built-in fact-checking against a source of truth
It is copying errors from a corrupted database
This only happens with very old models

quiz.question: Why is 'next-token prediction at scale' a more useful mental model than 'search engine' for predicting LLM behavior?
options: Because it explains both fluent generation and confident fabrication as two sides of the same mechanism
Because search engines are technically identical to LLMs
Because it means the model always tells the truth
It isn't useful; both models are equivalent

title: Tokens, Context Windows, and Why They Matter
content: Language models don't read text character by character or word by word -- they read tokens, chunks of text produced by a tokenizer (commonly byte-pair encoding), where a token might be a whole common word, a word fragment, or even a single punctuation mark. This course explains why 'the quick brown fox' might be 4 tokens while an uncommon word like 'antidisestablishmentarianism' could be split into 6 or more, and why this matters for both cost (providers bill per token) and behavior (models can be worse at character-level tasks like counting letters, because they never see individual characters). You'll also learn what a context window is: the maximum number of tokens (input plus output combined, for most APIs) a model can process in one call, and what happens when you exceed it -- either an error, or silent truncation of the oldest content, depending on the system. You'll leave able to estimate roughly how many tokens a piece of text will consume and explain why a bigger context window isn't free: it increases both cost and, past a point, the risk that the model pays less attention to content buried in the middle.

sections.heading: How Byte-Pair Encoding Turns Text Into Tokens
sections.body: Tokenizers don't guess at meaning -- they run a fixed algorithm learned once from a huge corpus. Byte-pair encoding (BPE) starts with individual characters (or raw bytes) and repeatedly merges whatever adjacent pair shows up most often in the training data into a single new unit, thousands of times, until it has built a vocabulary -- typically 50,000 to 100,000 entries for models like GPT-4 or Claude. Common English words like 'the', 'quick', 'brown', and 'fox' each appear so often that they earned their own single token early in this merging process, which is why 'the quick brown fox' comes out to about 4 tokens. A rare, morphologically complex word like 'antidisestablishmentarianism' never appeared often enough as a whole unit to earn a single token, so the tokenizer falls back to smaller pieces it does recognize -- something like 'anti', 'dis', 'establish', 'ment', 'arian', 'ism' -- six or more fragments stitched together. The vocabulary is fixed at training time, so every input, no matter how novel, gets forced through this same lookup process.

sections.heading: Why Token Boundaries Break Character-Level Reasoning
sections.body: Because the model's entire input is a sequence of token IDs -- integers pointing into that 50,000-to-100,000-entry vocabulary -- it never actually sees the letters inside a token as separate symbols. The token for 'strawberry' is one opaque ID; the model has no built-in mechanism for decomposing it back into s-t-r-a-w-b-e-r-r-y the way you would to count the r's. It can sometimes get character-level answers right by having memorized spelling patterns during training or by reasoning step-by-step out loud, but it's working against its own representation, not with it. This is the direct explanation for the classic failure mode of LLMs botching letter-counting, spelling, or reversing a word: the task requires character-level access, but the model's native unit of perception is the token, and token boundaries rarely line up with character boundaries at all.

sections.heading: Estimating Token Counts and Why Providers Bill This Way
sections.body: A workable rule of thumb for English prose: roughly 4 characters or about three-quarters of a word per token, so a 500-word page runs about 650-700 tokens, and a 100,000-word novel is on the order of 130,000-140,000 tokens. Code, non-English languages, and text with lots of rare words or symbols tokenize less efficiently -- sometimes 1.5-2x as many tokens per character -- because BPE's vocabulary was built mostly from common web and book text. This matters commercially because every major API bills per token, with separate (and different) rates for input versus output tokens -- output is often several times more expensive than input per token. A prompt padded with unnecessary boilerplate, or a system that re-sends the entire conversation history on every turn, directly multiplies your bill, which is why token-efficient prompting is a real engineering concern, not a nicety.

sections.heading: What a Context Window Actually Limits
sections.body: The context window is the hard ceiling on how many tokens a single API call can involve, and for most chat-style APIs that ceiling covers input and output combined -- your system prompt, conversation history, retrieved documents, and the model's reply all draw from the same shared budget. A model advertised with a 128,000-token context window doesn't give you 128,000 tokens of input plus another 128,000 of output; if your prompt consumes 127,500 tokens, the model has only 500 tokens left to generate a response before hitting the limit. What happens when you try to exceed it depends on the system: some APIs reject the call outright with an explicit error, while others -- particularly chat applications managing a running conversation -- silently drop or truncate the oldest messages to make room, which can quietly erase context the user assumed was still available.

sections.heading: The Hidden Cost of a Bigger Context Window
sections.body: It's tempting to treat a larger context window as pure upside -- just stuff in more documents, more history, more examples -- but it isn't free on two fronts. First, cost scales directly with tokens used: filling a 200,000-token window on every call, even when much of it is repeated boilerplate, multiplies your per-request bill regardless of whether the model needed all that material. Second, and less obvious, is an attention effect often called 'lost in the middle': empirical studies of long-context models show retrieval accuracy is highest for information near the very start or very end of the input and measurably drops for facts buried in the middle of a long context, even though the model technically 'saw' every token. So doubling your context window can simultaneously double your bill and make the model less reliable at using content stashed in the middle of that window -- a real design tradeoff, not just a bigger free lunch.

quiz.question: Why can an LLM sometimes struggle with a task like counting the letters in a word?
options: It never learned the alphabet
It processes text as tokens, which often don't correspond to individual characters
It's a hardware limitation
This never actually happens

quiz.question: What typically happens when your input plus expected output would exceed a model's context window?
options: The model automatically upgrades itself
You get an error or the oldest content gets silently truncated, depending on the system
Nothing, all systems handle this perfectly by default
The model pauses and waits for more memory

quiz.question: Why isn't a bigger context window simply 'free' upside with no downside?
options: Larger context windows are illegal in some countries
It increases cost and can increase the risk the model pays less attention to content buried in the middle
Bigger context windows make the model slower to install
There is no downside, bigger is strictly better

title: Choosing the Right Model for the Job
content: There is no single 'best' model -- only the best model for a given task, latency budget, and cost target. This course walks through a practical decision framework: start with task complexity (a simple classification or extraction task rarely needs a frontier reasoning model), then consider latency requirements (a real-time chat interface has very different tolerance than a nightly batch job), then cost at your expected volume (a 10x cost difference matters enormously at scale and barely at all for a prototype), then special requirements like reliable structured output, tool-calling ability, or a very long context window. You'll learn why teams frequently over-provision -- reaching for the largest, most expensive model by default -- and why a smaller model with a well-engineered prompt and good few-shot examples often matches a frontier model's accuracy on a narrow, well-specified task at a fraction of the cost and latency. You'll also learn to recognize the opposite mistake: under-provisioning on tasks that genuinely require strong multi-step reasoning, where a cheaper model fails silently by producing plausible-looking but wrong output.

sections.heading: Step 1: Start with Task Complexity, Not Brand Reputation
sections.body: Before touching a pricing page, characterize what the task actually demands. A binary classifier (is this support ticket a refund request?), a named-entity extraction task, or a template-filling job is bounded and narrow -- the output space is small and the reasoning required is shallow. These tasks rarely need a frontier model's multi-step reasoning or broad world knowledge; they need consistent adherence to a pattern. Contrast that with tasks requiring chained inference -- reconciling contradictory information across several documents, planning a multi-tool workflow, or debugging why two numbers in a spreadsheet don't match. Those need a model that can hold and manipulate several dependent facts at once without dropping one. The test: write out the task in one sentence and ask whether a competent junior employee with a one-page instruction sheet could do it correctly nine times out of ten. If yes, it's probably a small-model task. If it requires judgment calls across ambiguous, conflicting inputs, lean toward stronger reasoning capability.

sections.heading: Step 2: Latency Budgets Change the Model Shortlist
sections.body: The same task can have wildly different acceptable latencies depending on where it sits in your product. A synchronous chat UI where a user is watching a cursor blink needs a first-token response in well under a second and full completion in a few seconds at most -- that rules out large reasoning models with long deliberation chains, or at least forces you toward streaming and smaller variants. A background job that classifies 50,000 support tickets overnight has essentially no latency constraint at the per-item level; you can trade 2 extra seconds per call for meaningfully better accuracy since nothing is waiting on it synchronously. Voice interfaces are the tightest budget of all -- round-trip latency above roughly 300-500ms starts to feel like an awkward pause rather than natural conversation. Map your use case onto this spectrum before you compare benchmark scores, because a model that's technically more capable but doubles your response time can make a product feel broken even when every answer is correct.

sections.heading: Step 3: Cost at Volume -- Why a 10x Multiplier Matters or Doesn't
sections.body: Per-call cost differences that look trivial in a demo become the dominant line item at scale. A frontier model might run several times to over ten times the per-million-token price of a smaller sibling. At 100 calls a day during a pilot, that difference is a rounding error -- a few dollars a month either way, not worth engineering effort to optimize. At 10 million calls a month in production, the same ratio is the difference between a four-figure and a five- or six-figure monthly bill. The right move is to model cost as a function of your actual or projected volume curve, not a snapshot: prototype with whatever gets you signal fastest, but before committing to production architecture, price out the target model at 10x and 100x your current volume. If the numbers make you flinch, that's the signal to invest in prompt engineering, distillation, or a cheaper model rather than eating the frontier price forever.

sections.heading: Step 4: Special Requirements That Override the Default Choice
sections.body: Complexity, latency, and cost set the baseline shortlist, but certain requirements can force a specific model regardless of what the framework above suggests. Reliable structured output -- JSON that validates against a schema on every single call, not 95% of the time -- varies significantly across models and providers; some support constrained decoding or grammar-based sampling that guarantees schema conformance, others rely on prompting alone and will occasionally emit malformed or truncated JSON under load. Tool-calling ability matters when the model needs to chain multiple function calls with correct argument formatting across a multi-turn agentic loop -- weaker models can call the right tool but botch argument types or hallucinate parameters that don't exist. Context window matters when your task genuinely requires attending to a large amount of input at once, like summarizing a 200-page contract or reasoning over an entire codebase, rather than the more common case where a shorter window plus retrieval would do the same job for less.

sections.heading: The Two Provisioning Failure Modes: Over and Under
sections.body: Over-provisioning is the default failure mode for most teams: reaching for the largest, most expensive, most capable model regardless of task, because it's the safe-feeling choice and nobody gets blamed for picking the best. The cost is invisible until volume hits production and the bill arrives, and the latency cost is often absorbed silently by users who assume the product is just slow. The less obvious failure is under-provisioning -- picking a cheap, fast model for a task that actually requires genuine multi-step reasoning, like verifying that a proposed solution satisfies several interacting constraints. Weak models don't typically fail loudly here; they produce fluent, confident, plausible-looking output that is simply wrong, and because it reads well, it slips past review far more often than an obvious error would. Both failure modes are corrected the same way: benchmark candidate models against a held-out set of real examples from your actual task, including adversarial or edge cases, before locking in a choice based on general reputation alone.

quiz.question: Why might a smaller, cheaper model be the right choice for a narrow, well-specified task?
options: Smaller models are always more accurate
With good prompting and examples, a smaller model can match a frontier model's accuracy on narrow tasks at much lower cost and latency
Larger models cannot be used for simple tasks at all
This is never true in practice

quiz.question: What is a common mistake teams make when selecting a model?
options: Always choosing the cheapest option regardless of task
Over-provisioning by defaulting to the largest, most expensive model even for simple tasks
Never considering latency at all
Testing multiple models before committing

quiz.question: What is a risk of under-provisioning on a task that requires genuine multi-step reasoning?
options: The system will always crash with a visible error
The cheaper model may fail silently, producing plausible-looking but incorrect output
Nothing, cost is the only relevant factor
The task will simply run faster

title: Reading a Model Card
content: A model card is a provider's documentation summarizing a model's training data, intended uses, known limitations, benchmark performance, and safety evaluations -- and learning to read one critically is a core skill for picking models responsibly. This course covers what to look for: training data composition and cutoff date (does it know about recent events or your domain's jargon), stated intended use and out-of-scope uses (a model card explicitly warning against medical or legal advice use is a real signal, not boilerplate), and benchmark scores presented with context (a leaderboard number without knowing which exact benchmark version, whether the test set could have leaked into training data, or whether the benchmark measures anything relevant to your use case, is close to meaningless on its own). You'll also learn to look for license terms, since some 'open' models restrict commercial use or require attribution, and safety evaluation summaries, which tell you what red-teaming was done and what failure modes are already known before you ever run the model yourself.

sections.heading: Training Data Composition and Knowledge Cutoff
sections.body: Start with the data section, since it bounds everything else the card claims. Look for what the corpus actually contains -- web scrapes like Common Crawl or C4, licensed books and news, code repositories, synthetic data generated by another model -- and in what rough proportions. A card that just says 'a mix of publicly available and licensed data' with no breakdown is giving you almost nothing to work with; a card that names specific sources and percentages lets you reason about gaps. The cutoff date matters just as much: a model trained through early 2024 will not know a library API that shipped in 2025, will not recognize a company that renamed itself last year, and may confidently fabricate an answer rather than say so. If your use case leans on recent events, niche technical jargon, or a language underrepresented in web-scale corpora, the data section tells you upfront whether you are fighting the model's blind spots.

sections.heading: Intended Use vs. Out-of-Scope Use
sections.body: Following the Mitchell et al. model card framework, most cards separate 'intended use' from 'out-of-scope use,' and the second list is the one worth reading closely. When a provider writes that the model is not intended for medical diagnosis, legal advice, or autonomous high-stakes decisions, that is not reflexive liability-shielding boilerplate -- it usually reflects a specific known failure mode, such as elevated hallucination rates on clinical QA benchmarks or an absence of domain-expert review during fine-tuning. Conversely, if a card lists 'coding assistance' or 'customer support drafting' as intended uses, that signals the provider actually evaluated the model on tasks resembling those. Treat a detailed out-of-scope list as evidence the provider tested failure modes and found real ones; treat a vague or missing one as an unknown, not a clean bill of health.

sections.heading: Reading Benchmark Scores With Context, Not at Face Value
sections.body: A single leaderboard number like '88% on MMLU' tells you almost nothing without three pieces of context. First, which exact benchmark version and evaluation harness -- MMLU vs. MMLU-Pro, zero-shot vs. five-shot vs. chain-of-thought prompting can swing scores by 10-20 points on the same model. Second, contamination: benchmark question sets circulate on the open web and can leak into pretraining corpora, so a suspiciously high score on a well-known public benchmark deserves more scrutiny than a modest score on a held-out or provider-run eval. Third, relevance -- a strong HumanEval coding score says nothing about summarization quality or multilingual reasoning. Good cards report the harness version, few-shot setting, and ideally compare against a decontaminated or held-out variant; cards that just post a bare number next to a competitor's are asking you to take it on faith.

sections.heading: License Terms and Commercial Use Restrictions
sections.body: Open weights do not mean an open license, and this is one of the most consequential things to check before you build anything on top of a model. Meta's Llama community license, for example, is free to use but caps out at 700 million monthly active users and requires 'Built with Llama' attribution above that threshold -- a real constraint for a growing product. Other 'open' releases use RAIL-style licenses that restrict specific use cases (surveillance, certain commercial applications) regardless of scale, while genuinely permissive licenses like Apache 2.0 or MIT impose no such conditions. Before you assume you can deploy a model in a commercial product, read the actual license text on the model card, not just the marketing language calling it 'open source' -- the two words are used loosely across the industry and the gap between them can be a legal problem later.

sections.heading: Safety Evaluations and Documented Failure Modes
sections.body: The safety section tells you what the provider already knows is broken so you don't have to discover it in production. Look for red-teaming summaries -- adversarial prompts designed to elicit jailbreaks, toxic output, or policy violations -- along with quantified results, such as a stated reduction in harmful response rate after RLHF or a refusal-rate table across categories like violence, self-harm, or biased content. Bias evaluations against benchmarks like BBQ or Winogender indicate the provider tested for demographic stereotyping rather than assuming it away. A card that is silent on safety testing entirely is not evidence of a clean model; it usually means the evaluation either was not done or was not disclosed, and either way you are the one who now owns discovering the failure modes.

quiz.question: Why should a benchmark score on a model card be read with skepticism rather than taken at face value?
options: Benchmark scores are always fabricated
Without knowing the exact benchmark, possible test-set contamination, and relevance to your use case, the number alone tells you little
Benchmarks never change over time
Model cards don't include benchmarks

quiz.question: Why does a model card's 'out-of-scope uses' section matter?
options: It's just legal boilerplate with no practical meaning
It signals real limitations, like explicitly warning against medical or legal advice use
It only applies to open-weight models
It replaces the need for any testing

quiz.question: What should you check on a model card before assuming you can use a model commercially?
options: The color scheme of the documentation
The license terms, since some 'open' models restrict commercial use
The number of parameters only
Nothing, all models can be used commercially

title: Open-Weight vs. Closed Models
content: Open-weight models (like Llama or Mistral) publish their trained parameters for anyone to download, run, and fine-tune, while closed models (like GPT, Claude, or Gemini) are only accessible through a provider's API. This course covers the real tradeoffs behind that choice: open-weight models give you full control over hosting, data privacy (nothing leaves your infrastructure), and the ability to fine-tune on proprietary data, at the cost of you owning all the infrastructure, scaling, and reliability engineering yourself. Closed models typically offer the most capable frontier performance and zero infrastructure burden, but you're sending data to a third party, subject to their rate limits, pricing changes, and deprecation schedules. You'll learn a key nuance often missed: 'open' doesn't always mean 'free to use however you want' -- some open-weight licenses restrict commercial use above a certain scale or require attribution, so the licensing terms matter as much as the technical access model. You'll leave able to match a project's constraints (data sensitivity, budget, need for customization, team's infra capacity) to the right category.

sections.heading: What 'Open-Weight' Actually Gives You Access To
sections.body: Open-weight means the trained parameters -- the actual matrices of numbers produced by pretraining and fine-tuning -- are published as downloadable files, typically as safetensors checkpoints ranging from a few hundred MB for a small model up to hundreds of GB for something like Llama 3.1 405B. You get the weights, usually a tokenizer, and sometimes a reference inference script, but critically you do NOT get the training data, the training code, or the compute recipe used to produce the model. That's why 'open-weight' and 'open-source' aren't synonyms: a true open-source model would let you reproduce it from scratch, while an open-weight model is more like getting a compiled binary with permission to run and modify it, not the source code that built it. Closed models like GPT-4-class or Claude give you none of this -- you send a prompt over HTTPS to an endpoint and get tokens back, with the weights themselves never leaving the provider's infrastructure. This distinction matters operationally: with open weights you can inspect the architecture (layer count, attention type, context window implementation), quantize it yourself, or splice in a custom tokenizer, none of which is possible against an API.

sections.heading: The Infrastructure Bill Nobody Mentions Until You're Paying It
sections.body: Downloading a model file is the easy 5% of self-hosting. The hard 95% is everything around it: provisioning GPUs (a 70B-parameter model needs roughly 140GB of VRAM at fp16, meaning at least two or three A100/H100 80GB cards, or heavy quantization down to 4-bit to squeeze onto one), running an inference server like vLLM or TGI that handles batching and KV-cache management efficiently, setting up autoscaling so you're not paying for idle GPUs at 3am, and building monitoring for latency, throughput, and GPU memory pressure. You also inherit the reliability engineering: if a node dies mid-request, you need retry logic and failover, because there's no SLA-backed provider absorbing that for you. Closed APIs collapse all of this into a single HTTP call with a published uptime SLA -- you trade a recurring infra headcount cost for a per-token price and someone else's ops team. The breakeven point is usually volume-driven: at low request volume, API pricing per million tokens beats amortized GPU cost, but at sustained high volume, self-hosting can become cheaper even after counting the engineering time, especially once you factor in that idle rented GPUs cost money whether or not a request is in flight.

sections.heading: Data Privacy and Residency: Why Self-Hosting Changes the Threat Model
sections.body: When you call a closed model's API, your prompt -- which may include customer PII, proprietary source code, or unreleased financial data -- leaves your network boundary and transits to a third party. Most providers offer contractual guarantees (zero data retention modes, enterprise agreements that exclude your traffic from training) but you're trusting their implementation and their subprocessors, and some regulated industries (healthcare under HIPAA, EU data under GDPR's data-residency rules, government contracts requiring FedRAMP) simply prohibit sending certain data to external endpoints at all, regardless of contractual promises. Self-hosting an open-weight model inside your own VPC or on-prem cluster means the data never crosses a boundary you don't control -- inference happens on your hardware, in your region, under your existing compliance posture, so a HIPAA risk assessment or a data-residency audit doesn't need to account for an external processor at all. This is frequently the deciding factor even when the closed model is measurably more capable: a team bound by strict data-residency requirements with existing in-house ML infrastructure will typically choose a self-hosted open-weight model specifically to keep every byte of sensitive data inside their own walls, accepting somewhat lower benchmark scores as the cost of that guarantee.

sections.heading: Reading Licenses: Llama, Mistral, Apache 2.0, and the Fine Print
sections.body: The word 'open' hides real legal variation. Meta's Llama license, for instance, is not OSI-approved open source -- it's a custom license that requires any company with more than 700 million monthly active users to obtain a separate commercial license from Meta, and it carries acceptable-use restrictions on certain applications. Some earlier community fine-tunes and research-only releases (e.g., certain Qwen or research checkpoints) forbid commercial use entirely, permitting only research or personal experimentation. Contrast that with Mistral's Apache 2.0-licensed models or Apache/MIT-licensed releases generally, which impose essentially no restriction beyond attribution and a disclaimer of warranty -- you can fine-tune, redistribute, and sell a product built on them with no revenue threshold or use-case carve-out. The practical failure mode is teams assuming 'downloadable weights' equals 'free to use however we want' and only discovering the attribution requirement or the scale-based commercial trigger during a legal review months into a product's life. Before building on any open-weight model, read the actual license text (not just the model card summary) for: commercial-use permission, any user-count or revenue threshold, attribution requirements, and restrictions on specific downstream uses -- these vary release to release even from the same vendor.

sections.heading: Matching the Model Category to Your Project's Real Constraints
sections.body: In practice this decision comes down to four questions, in roughly this priority order. First, data sensitivity: if you're handling regulated or highly confidential data and can't get comfortable with a third-party processor regardless of their SLA, self-hosted open-weight wins by default. Second, budget shape: sporadic, low-volume usage favors a closed API's pay-per-token model with zero upfront cost, while high, steady-state volume favors amortizing GPU infrastructure. Third, need for deep customization: if you need to fine-tune on proprietary data at a level beyond what an API's fine-tuning endpoint exposes, or need to modify the architecture itself (custom attention windows, merged adapters, quantization schemes), only open weights give you that surface area. Fourth, team infrastructure capacity: an org without anyone who has run GPU inference in production will burn months of runway just getting a self-hosted stack reliable, making a closed API the pragmatic choice even when the other three factors point toward open-weight. Most real decisions aren't unanimous across these four axes, which is exactly why treating it as a single 'open vs. closed' binary rather than a per-project fit exercise leads teams astray.

quiz.question: What is a key benefit of open-weight models over closed API-only models?
options: They are always more accurate
They give you control over hosting and data privacy since nothing needs to leave your infrastructure
They never have any licensing restrictions
They require no engineering effort at all

quiz.question: What is a common misconception about 'open' models?
options: That they are all trained the same way
That 'open' always means unrestricted commercial use, when some licenses restrict scale or require attribution
That they can never be fine-tuned
That they are always smaller than closed models

quiz.question: A team has strict data-residency requirements and in-house ML infrastructure. Which model category is likely a better fit?
options: A closed API-only model, regardless of requirements
An open-weight model they can self-host to keep data in-house
Neither option can satisfy data-residency requirements
The choice has no bearing on data residency

title: How LLMs Generate Text: Autoregression and Sampling
content: LLMs generate text one token at a time, feeding each generated token back in as input to predict the next one -- a process called autoregressive generation. At each step, the model produces a probability distribution over its entire vocabulary (via a softmax function), and a sampling strategy decides which token to actually pick. This course covers the key sampling parameters that shape output: temperature (scaling the distribution -- low temperature makes the model pick high-probability tokens almost deterministically, high temperature flattens the distribution toward more surprising, creative choices), top-p / nucleus sampling (only sampling from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds p, cutting off the unlikely long tail), and top-k (restricting sampling to only the k most likely tokens). You'll learn why 'hallucination' is not a separate bug bolted onto an otherwise-truthful system, but a natural consequence of a model that is always generating the statistically plausible next token -- there is no built-in step where it checks generated content against ground truth, so a fluent, grammatically perfect sentence can still be entirely fabricated.

sections.heading: Autoregressive Generation: One Token at a Time
sections.body: An LLM never writes a sentence in one shot. It generates a single token, appends that token to its input, and runs the whole forward pass again to predict the next one -- this loop is what 'autoregressive' means (the model regresses on its own prior output). Given 'The cat sat on the', the model predicts 'mat' as the next token, then the input becomes 'The cat sat on the mat' and it predicts again, perhaps a period or an end-of-sequence token that stops the loop. Because each step depends on every token generated so far, generation is inherently sequential -- you cannot skip ahead to token 50 without first producing tokens 1 through 49. This is also why longer outputs take proportionally longer to generate and why a model can 'paint itself into a corner': once a token is chosen and fed back in, it becomes fixed context that shapes everything that follows, even if a different early choice would have led somewhere better.

sections.heading: From Logits to Probabilities: The Softmax Step
sections.body: At each generation step, the model's final layer doesn't output a token directly -- it outputs a raw score, called a logit, for every entry in its vocabulary. A modern LLM's vocabulary typically has 32,000 to over 100,000 possible tokens (GPT-style tokenizers commonly sit around 100k; Llama's is roughly 32k), so this is a single vector of that many numbers, and they can be any real value, positive or negative. Softmax converts this vector into a valid probability distribution: it exponentiates each logit, then divides by the sum of all the exponentiated values, so the results are all positive and sum to exactly 1. A token with a much higher logit than the rest ends up with probability close to 1; a crowded field of similar logits produces a flatter spread across many plausible next tokens. Everything downstream -- temperature, top-k, top-p -- operates on this distribution, either before or after the softmax reshapes it.

sections.heading: Temperature: Turning Up or Down the Randomness
sections.body: Temperature is applied before softmax: every logit is divided by the temperature value T before exponentiating. At T=1, the distribution is unchanged from the model's raw prediction. As T drops below 1 (say 0.2), dividing by a small number stretches the gaps between logits, so the softmax output concentrates almost all probability mass on the single best token -- generation becomes close to deterministic, favoring safe, high-confidence continuations, which is desirable for tasks like code generation or factual Q&A. As T rises above 1 (say 1.3), dividing by a large number compresses the gaps between logits, flattening the distribution so lower-probability tokens get a real chance of being sampled -- output becomes more varied and surprising, useful for brainstorming or creative writing, but also more prone to incoherence if pushed too far. Temperature never adds tokens that weren't already candidates; it only reshapes how sharply the existing distribution favors the top choices.

sections.heading: Top-k and Top-p (Nucleus) Sampling: Trimming the Long Tail
sections.body: Even after temperature scaling, a full vocabulary distribution still assigns some nonzero probability to tens of thousands of nonsensical tokens -- sampling directly from that raw distribution occasionally produces garbage. Top-k sampling fixes this by keeping only the k tokens with the highest probability (say k=40), discarding everything else, and renormalizing before sampling -- simple, but k is a fixed count regardless of how the probability is actually distributed. Top-p (nucleus) sampling instead keeps the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds a threshold p (say 0.9): when the model is very confident, that nucleus might contain just 2-3 tokens; when it's uncertain, the nucleus might need 50 tokens to reach 0.9, so the candidate pool adapts to the shape of the distribution rather than staying fixed. Production APIs commonly apply temperature, then top-k, then top-p in sequence, each one narrowing the field before the final random draw.

sections.heading: Why Hallucination Is a Feature of the Process, Not a Bug in It
sections.body: It's tempting to think of hallucination as a defect that occasional escapes an otherwise truth-checking system, but there is no truth-checking system to escape from. At every single step, the model is doing exactly one thing: computing a probability distribution over 'what token is statistically plausible next, given my training data and the text so far' and sampling from it. There is no separate module that pauses generation to verify a claimed date, a cited paper, or a function signature against reality -- fluency and factual accuracy are produced by the same undifferentiated mechanism, so a confident, grammatically flawless sentence can be entirely fabricated if a plausible-sounding but false continuation happened to score well. This is precisely why mitigations like retrieval-augmented generation, citations, or explicit fact-checking passes are bolted on from the outside as separate systems, rather than being a setting you flip on inside the sampler -- temperature and top-p control how creative or safe the wording is, but neither one has any concept of what is true.

options: The model generates the entire response at once
The model generates one token at a time, feeding each output back in to predict the next
The model only works on regression problems, not text
The model regenerates its own weights during inference

quiz.question: What effect does a higher temperature setting have on generation?
options: It makes the model deterministic and always pick the single most likely token
It flattens the probability distribution, increasing the chance of more surprising or creative token choices
It has no effect on output at all
It only affects how fast tokens are generated

quiz.question: Why is hallucination best understood as a natural consequence of how LLMs generate text, rather than a separate bug?
options: Because the model is deliberately programmed to lie
Because the model always generates the statistically plausible next token with no built-in fact-check against ground truth
Because hallucination only occurs due to hardware errors
Because it only happens with very small models

title: Prompting Basics: Structure, Examples, and Output Format
content: A well-structured prompt reliably improves output quality more than almost any other lever available to you, and this course covers the foundational structure: clear task instructions stated up front, relevant context the model needs to complete the task, and an explicit description of the desired output format (a JSON schema, a specific list length, a tone). You'll learn about few-shot prompting -- including one or more worked examples of input-and-desired-output pairs directly in the prompt -- and why it often outperforms lengthy abstract instructions, because showing the model exactly what 'good' looks like removes ambiguity that a written description can leave open. You'll also learn the difference between a system prompt (persistent instructions that apply across a whole conversation, like persona or constraints) and a user prompt (the specific task or question at hand) at a high level -- this course introduces the distinction, while the Context Engineering track goes deeper on how to actually architect what goes into each. A recurring theme: specificity beats generality; a vague instruction like 'be helpful' produces far less consistent output than a precise one describing exactly what a good answer contains.

sections.heading: The Three-Part Anatomy of a Working Prompt
sections.body: Almost every prompt that reliably produces good output has the same three ingredients, in roughly this order. First, the task instruction: a direct statement of what you want done, phrased as an imperative -- "summarize this contract's termination clauses" beats "can you help me understand this document?" Second, context: the specific material the model needs and nothing more -- the contract text itself, a customer's prior messages, a database schema, the relevant rows rather than the whole table. Models don't know what you know; if a fact matters to the answer, it has to be in the prompt. Third, the output format: how the response should be shaped, not just what it should contain. Leaving any one of these three out doesn't make the model fail outright, but it makes the output unpredictable -- you get a plausible-sounding response that may not be the one you actually needed, and you end up iterating in the chat window instead of getting it right the first time.

sections.heading: Specifying Output Format So You Don't Have to Parse Prose
sections.body: The output-format instruction is the piece people skip most often, and it's the one with the biggest payoff when you're building anything that consumes the model's response programmatically. "Give me a list of action items" produces a different shape every time -- sometimes numbered, sometimes bulleted, sometimes buried in a paragraph. "Return a JSON array of objects, each with 'task' (string) and 'owner' (string, or null if unassigned)" produces the same shape every time, because you've described the schema instead of hoping the model infers it. The same logic applies to non-JSON constraints: "exactly three bullet points, each under 15 words" or "respond in the tone of a terse engineering changelog, no adjectives." The rule of thumb: if you can describe the shape you want, describe it explicitly in the prompt -- don't leave the model to guess a default format and then write code to clean up whatever it happens to produce.

sections.heading: Few-Shot Prompting: Show, Don't Just Tell
sections.body: A few-shot prompt embeds one or more worked examples -- an input paired with the exact output you'd consider correct -- directly in the prompt, before the model sees the real input it has to handle. This often beats even a carefully written paragraph of abstract instructions, for a simple reason: written descriptions leave interpretive gaps. "Write a concise, professional email" leaves 'concise' and 'professional' open to the model's own judgment, which varies response to response. Two examples of actual emails you'd sign off on close that gap immediately -- the model can pattern-match length, tone, structure, and level of formality from the examples themselves rather than reconstructing them from adjectives. In practice, two to three diverse examples (covering edge cases, not just the typical case) is usually enough; more than that mostly adds token cost without much added consistency, and examples that are all near-identical don't teach the model where the boundaries of 'correct' actually are.

sections.heading: System Prompts vs. User Prompts
sections.body: Most LLM APIs let you send a system prompt and a user prompt as separate fields, and the distinction matters even before you get into more advanced context architecture. The system prompt holds instructions meant to persist across an entire conversation or session: the model's persona ("you are a terse senior code reviewer"), standing constraints ("never suggest deleting data, only flag it"), and formatting defaults that should apply to every turn, not just the current one. The user prompt is the specific ask for this particular turn -- the question, the document to summarize, the code to review right now. Splitting them this way means you don't have to restate the persona and constraints in every single message, and it keeps the model's behavior stable across a long back-and-forth instead of drifting as the conversation grows. This course only introduces the split at this level; the Context Engineering track covers how to actually decide what belongs in each field as prompts and applications get more complex.

sections.heading: Why Vague Instructions Produce Inconsistent Output
sections.body: "Be helpful" is the canonical example of an instruction that sounds reasonable and produces wildly inconsistent results, because it hands the model an underspecified goal and forces it to guess what 'helpful' means in this specific context. Sometimes that guess is a two-line answer, sometimes a five-paragraph essay with caveats, sometimes a bulleted list nobody asked for -- all technically 'helpful,' none of them predictable. Compare that to "answer in two sentences, state the direct recommendation first, then one sentence of reasoning": there's no ambiguity left for the model to resolve on its own, so repeated runs converge on essentially the same shape of answer. The general pattern holds everywhere in prompting -- 'good code,' 'thorough,' 'professional tone' are all vague in exactly this way. Naming precisely what a good answer contains, or showing an example of one, is what actually removes the guesswork -- generality is what invites it.

options: Examples are always shorter than instructions
Showing exactly what 'good' output looks like removes ambiguity that written descriptions can leave open

options: There is no difference
A system prompt holds persistent instructions/persona across a conversation, while a user prompt is the specific task at hand
A system prompt is always shorter than a user prompt

quiz.question: Why does a vague instruction like 'be helpful' tend to produce less consistent output than a specific one?
options: Vague instructions are technically invalid JSON
It leaves the model to guess what 'helpful' means in this context, versus a precise description of what a good answer contains

title: Fine-Tuning vs. Prompting vs. RAG: Choosing the Right Lever
content: Teams often reach for fine-tuning to solve problems that prompting or RAG would solve faster and cheaper, and this course builds the judgment to tell them apart. Prompt engineering (including few-shot examples) is fast to iterate, requires no training infrastructure, and is the right first step for most problems, especially ones about format, tone, or task framing. RAG is the right tool when the problem is 'the model doesn't know this specific fact or this changed recently' -- it injects fresh, retrievable knowledge without touching the model's weights. Fine-tuning changes the model's weights on a custom dataset, and it's the right tool for a narrower set of problems: teaching a very consistent output style or format the model doesn't reliably produce even with good prompting, adapting to a specialized vocabulary or writing style at scale, or reducing prompt length (and therefore cost) for a repeated task once you know the exact desired behavior. You'll learn the common mistake: fine-tuning on facts, hoping the model will 'know' new information reliably -- fine-tuning is poor at reliably injecting new factual knowledge and terrible at keeping that knowledge current, which is exactly what RAG is built for instead.

sections.heading: Prompt Engineering: The Default First Move
sections.body: Prompting -- including zero-shot instructions, few-shot examples, and structured system prompts -- should be your default hypothesis for almost any behavior problem, because the iteration loop is a single API call, not a training run. You can test a reworded instruction or a new few-shot example in seconds and roll it back just as fast if it regresses. This makes prompting the cheapest possible experiment for diagnosing what's actually wrong. Most failures that look like 'the model doesn't understand the task' are actually framing problems: the instructions are ambiguous, the desired output format isn't specified precisely enough, or there aren't enough examples showing edge cases. Adding 3-5 well-chosen few-shot examples that cover the tricky cases (not just the easy ones) resolves a surprising share of format and tone complaints outright. Only after you've genuinely exhausted prompting -- tried explicit formatting instructions, added examples, tried a different model, tried chain-of-thought scaffolding -- should you conclude the problem needs a different lever. Skipping this step is the single most common source of wasted engineering time in this space.

sections.heading: RAG: Solving 'The Model Doesn't Know This Fact'
sections.body: RAG earns its place when the failure mode is specifically epistemic: the model gives a wrong or outdated answer because the fact simply isn't in its parametric knowledge, or it changes too often to bake in. Think product catalogs updated weekly, internal policy docs, ticket histories, or anything with a last-modified date that matters. RAG solves this by retrieving relevant passages at query time -- via vector similarity search, BM25, or a hybrid of both -- and injecting them into the context window so the model reasons over ground-truth text it can cite, rather than recalling (and potentially hallucinating) from training-time memorization. The practical tell that you need RAG rather than fine-tuning: if you'd have to retrain weekly to keep the model current, that's a retrieval problem, not a weights problem. RAG also gives you provenance almost for free -- you can show the user which chunk the answer came from -- and lets you patch bad information immediately by editing the source document, with zero retraining latency. Fine-tuning offers none of that: baked-in facts go stale the moment the underlying reality changes.

sections.heading: Fine-Tuning: A Narrow Tool for Behavior, Not Facts
sections.body: Fine-tuning updates the model's weights via gradient descent on a curated dataset of input-output pairs (or preference pairs, for RLHF/DPO-style tuning), and it genuinely excels at exactly one category of problem: making a specific behavior more reliable and more compact to invoke. Concretely: a support-ticket classifier that needs a rigid JSON schema every single time with zero drift; a domain-specific writing style (legal boilerplate, medical charting shorthand) that few-shot prompting approximates but never nails consistently; or collapsing a 2,000-token system prompt plus ten few-shot examples down to a near-empty prompt once the desired behavior is baked into the weights, cutting per-call token cost and latency at scale. The tell that fine-tuning is the right lever: you already know, from prompting experiments, exactly what 'correct' looks like, the behavior needs to be nearly 100% consistent across thousands of calls, and the pattern itself is stable over time rather than something that changes weekly.

sections.heading: The Classic Mistake: Fine-Tuning to Teach New Facts
sections.body: The most expensive mistake teams make is fine-tuning a model on a document set -- a product manual, a knowledge base, a set of policies -- hoping the model will thereby 'know' those facts reliably going forward. This misunderstands what fine-tuning actually does to a transformer's weights: gradient updates on factual text nudge the model's general statistical tendencies, they don't create a reliable, addressable lookup table. The model may reproduce facts it saw often in training, paraphrase others incorrectly, and confidently hallucinate specifics it saw rarely or not at all -- with no way to tell which case you're in for any given query. Worse, the moment the underlying facts change, that fine-tuned knowledge is stale and you're stuck retraining on a rolling basis just to stay current, which is slow and expensive compared to editing a document in a retrieval index. If the requirement is 'the model must know X reliably, and X may change,' that is RAG's job description, not fine-tuning's. Reach for fine-tuning to shape behavior and style; reach for RAG to supply facts.

sections.heading: A Decision Framework: Diagnosing the Failure Before Picking a Lever
sections.body: Before choosing a lever, diagnose the failure precisely, because each lever fixes a different root cause. Ask three questions in order. First: is this about format, tone, or task framing -- something a clearer instruction or better few-shot example could fix? If yes, prompt first; it's nearly free to test. Second: is this about the model lacking specific knowledge, especially knowledge that could change next week or next quarter? If yes, that's RAG's job -- retrieval keeps you current without retraining. Third, only if both of those are ruled out: is the required behavior stable, well-understood from your prompting experiments, and needed at high volume with near-perfect consistency or lower token cost? Only then does fine-tuning pay for itself, since it requires a labeled dataset, training infrastructure or an API fine-tuning job, evaluation, and ongoing maintenance as the underlying task drifts. These levers also compose: a production RAG system commonly layers a fine-tuned or well-prompted generation model on top of a separately-optimized retrieval pipeline, using each lever for the failure mode it actually addresses.

options: Teaching a consistent output format
Reliably injecting new, frequently-changing factual knowledge into the model
Adapting to a specialized vocabulary
Reducing prompt length for a repeated task

options: When you need the model to know specific facts that change frequently over time

title: Embeddings Explained: Turning Meaning Into Vectors
content: An embedding model converts a piece of text into a fixed-length vector of numbers positioned so that semantically similar text ends up close together in that vector space -- 'a friendly dog' and 'a happy puppy' land nearer each other than either does to 'quarterly tax filing.' This course covers how embedding models are typically trained using contrastive learning (pulling similar pairs closer, pushing dissimilar pairs apart) and how the resulting vectors get used: similarity search (the backbone of RAG retrieval), clustering (grouping similar documents without labels), and classification (using vector distance to a set of labeled examples). You'll learn the important distinction between an embedding model and a generative LLM: an embedding model doesn't generate text at all, it only produces a numeric representation, and the two are often entirely different model architectures even when offered by the same provider. You'll also learn about the practical tradeoff in embedding dimensionality -- higher-dimensional vectors (1536 or more) can capture finer-grained distinctions but cost more to store and search, while smaller vectors (384-768) are cheaper and often sufficient for narrower domains.

sections.heading: Embedding Models vs. Generative LLMs: Two Different Jobs
sections.body: It's tempting to think of an embedding model as a smaller, cheaper cousin of a chatbot, but they solve different problems entirely. A generative LLM takes in tokens and produces more tokens -- it's an autoregressive decoder trained to predict the next word. An embedding model takes in tokens and produces a single fixed-length vector -- often the pooled or averaged output of an encoder's final hidden states -- and stops there. It never emits text; there's no decoding step, no sampling temperature, no next-token loop. This is why OpenAI, Cohere, and Google all ship embedding endpoints (text-embedding-3-small, embed-english-v3, gemini-embedding-001) that are architecturally distinct from their chat models, sometimes built on encoder-only transformers (like BERT-style bidirectional attention) rather than the decoder-only architecture powering GPT-style generation. You call an embedding model when you need a representation to compare, store, or search -- not when you need prose.

sections.heading: Contrastive Learning: Teaching a Model What 'Similar' Means
sections.body: Embedding models don't learn semantic similarity by accident -- it's the direct objective of training. The dominant approach is contrastive learning: the model is fed anchor-positive pairs (a question and its correct answer, two paraphrases of a sentence, a product title and a matching review) alongside negative examples that are unrelated. A loss function like InfoNCE or triplet loss then pulls the anchor and positive vectors closer together in the embedding space while pushing the anchor away from the negatives, usually measured with cosine similarity or dot product. Crucially, negatives matter more than positives for quality -- 'hard negatives' (text that's superficially similar but semantically different, like two sentences sharing keywords but different meanings) force the model to learn finer distinctions than easy negatives would. Models like Sentence-BERT, E5, and GTE are all trained this way, often on billions of mined pairs from sources like search-click logs, Q&A forums, and back-translated paraphrases.

sections.heading: Reading the Vector Space: Distance as Meaning
sections.body: Once trained, the embedding space has real geometric structure you can reason about. Take three phrases: 'a friendly dog', 'a happy puppy', and 'quarterly tax filing'. Run them through an embedding model and measure cosine similarity (the cosine of the angle between two vectors, ranging from -1 to 1, with 1 meaning identical direction) and you'll typically see something like 0.7-0.85 between the two dog phrases -- they share subject matter, positive sentiment, and a similar syntactic pattern -- versus 0.1-0.3 between either dog phrase and the tax filing text, which shares almost no semantic content. Nearby vectors aren't just 'related words' -- they capture paraphrase, topic, and even tone. This is what lets you do arithmetic-like reasoning in embedding space (the classic example being king - man + woman lands near queen in older word-vector models like word2vec) and what makes nearest-neighbor search a meaningful proxy for 'find text that means the same thing.'

sections.heading: What You Build on Top: Search, Clustering, and Classification
sections.body: Once text is a vector, three workhorse applications open up. Similarity search is the backbone of RAG: embed a user's query, embed your document chunks ahead of time, and retrieve the k nearest vectors (via cosine similarity or approximate nearest-neighbor indexes like HNSW or IVF in vector databases such as Pinecone, Weaviate, or pgvector) to pull relevant context into a prompt. Clustering groups vectors with no labels at all -- run k-means or HDBSCAN over thousands of support-ticket embeddings and you'll surface natural topic groups (billing issues, login problems, feature requests) without anyone tagging a single ticket. Classification repurposes distance itself as a decision rule: embed a handful of labeled examples per category, embed the new input, and assign it to whichever labeled centroid it's closest to -- a lightweight alternative to fine-tuning a classifier when you have few examples per class.

sections.heading: Choosing a Dimension Count: 384 vs. 1536 and Beyond
sections.body: Embedding vectors come in fixed sizes set by the model architecture -- common options run from 384 (all-MiniLM-L6-v2) up through 768, 1024, and 1536 or higher (text-embedding-3-large can go to 3072). More dimensions mean more capacity to encode fine-grained distinctions -- subtle differences in tone, domain-specific jargon, multi-topic documents -- but that capacity isn't free. Storage scales linearly (a million 1536-dim float32 vectors is roughly 6GB versus 1.5GB at 384 dimensions), and nearest-neighbor search over higher-dimensional indexes costs more in both memory and query latency. Newer models increasingly support Matryoshka Representation Learning, which trains a single embedding so its first N dimensions alone remain useful -- letting you truncate a 1536-dim vector down to 256 dimensions and still get reasonable similarity search, trading some accuracy for a large cut in storage and compute cost.
