This is why the fix is almost never "write a better description" -- the marginal tool description improvement can't overcome an option space that's fundamentally too large to reason over cleanly.

sections.heading: Tool Retrieval: Treating Tool Selection Like a RAG Problem
sections.body: Tool retrieval borrows the indexing/retrieval split from RAG directly. Offline, you embed each tool's name, description, and ideally a few example invocations or the kinds of user phrases that should trigger it, producing one vector per tool in your catalog. At request time, you embed the current user message (or a short rolling summary of the conversation) and run a nearest-neighbor search -- cosine similarity is standard -- against the tool vectors, then inject only the top-k, typically 5 to 10, into the actual tools parameter sent to the model. The rest of the catalog simply doesn't exist for that turn. The core risk is recall failure: if the embedding model doesn't capture that "my card got declined" should retrieve a tool named `retry_payment_method`, the agent will confidently claim it can't help, which is worse than slow. Two mitigations matter in practice: hybrid retrieval that combines embedding similarity with keyword/BM25 matching to catch exact-term queries embeddings miss, and a fallback meta-tool like `search_available_tools` the model can invoke explicitly when nothing in its current top-k fits, effectively giving it a second retrieval pass instead of failing silently. You also need a re-embedding step wired into your tool-catalog deployment pipeline, since a stale index quietly excludes newly added tools from ever being retrieved.

sections.heading: Hierarchical Tool Routing: Classify First, Expose Second
sections.body: Hierarchical routing front-loads a cheap classification step -- often a small, fast model call or even a single forced tool-choice against a fixed list of 5-10 broad categories like 'billing', 'scheduling', 'account', 'search' -- before the agent ever sees a tool schema. Only after the category is picked does the system expose that category's narrower toolset, which might be 3-8 tools instead of fifty. This is cheaper and more deterministic than retrieval: category taxonomies are small, human-auditable, and version-controllable, and a tiny classifier adds negligible latency compared to embedding search over a large catalog. The characteristic failure mode is requests that genuinely span categories -- "cancel my subscription and refund last month's charge" touches both billing and account tools -- where a rigid single-category router either picks one and misses the other, or needs a second routing pass once the first action completes. Production systems handle this by letting the router return more than one category when confidence is split, or by keeping a narrow always-visible core (like a 'switch_category' or 'escalate' tool) so the agent can request a broader set mid-conversation rather than being permanently locked into the first classification. The other risk is compounding error: a misrouted first step means every subsequent tool choice is drawn from the wrong pool entirely, so routing accuracy deserves its own evaluation set, separate from tool-selection accuracy within a category.

sections.heading: Toolset Grouping: Coarse, Rule-Based Bundles Instead of Per-Tool Scoring
sections.body: Toolset grouping skips relevance scoring entirely and instead bundles tools that are used together as a matter of workflow contract -- all calendar tools (`create_event`, `find_availability`, `cancel_event`) travel as one unit, enabled or disabled based on context like user role, active feature flag, or conversation topic, rather than each tool being independently judged relevant per turn. This trades adaptiveness for predictability: a group is either fully on or fully off, which makes behavior easier to test, version, and gate by permission (an 'admin toolset' that only admin-role sessions ever see, for instance), and it sidesteps retrieval's recall-failure risk since there's no similarity threshold that can silently exclude a needed tool. It works best when tool usage genuinely clusters by workflow -- a project-management agent's ticket tools are almost always used together regardless of the specific request -- and works poorly when tools that seem related are actually used independently, since bundling them defeats the purpose of trimming the surface. The other limitation is that grouping alone doesn't solve scale within a large group: if your 'billing' toolset itself has twenty tools, you've just moved the fifty-tool problem down one level, which is why grouping is frequently layered with retrieval or routing operating inside each group rather than treated as a standalone fix.

sections.heading: The Common Lever: Shrinking Option-Space, Not Improving Options
sections.body: Retrieval, hierarchical routing, and toolset grouping look like three different techniques, but they're the same lever pulled three different ways: each one reduces how much irrelevant tool surface the model has to filter through at the moment it decides what to call, rather than trying to make any individual tool's description sharper. That reframing matters for where you spend effort -- teams that hit a selection-accuracy wall and respond by rewriting tool descriptions are usually optimizing the wrong variable, since the bottleneck is the size of the option set, not the clarity of any one entry within it. In practice the three strategies compose rather than compete: route to a broad category cheaply, retrieve the top few candidates within that category's tools, and gate the whole bundle by a toolset flag tied to user permissions -- each layer trims the surface further before the model ever reasons about a specific call. When choosing among them, weigh the failure mode you can tolerate: retrieval risks silent recall misses, routing risks compounding misclassification, and grouping risks under-adaptiveness -- there's no strategy that eliminates the tradeoff, only ones that shift where the risk sits. Whatever combination you pick, measure tool-selection accuracy bucketed by how many tools were actually visible on a given turn, not just in aggregate, since that's the variable actually driving the error rate.

quiz.question: Why does an agent with fifty available tools tend to select the wrong one more often than an agent with five?
options: Larger tool counts always improve selection accuracy
The model has to reason about every tool's name, description, and schema at once, and more options increase the chance of picking wrong
Tool count has no effect on selection accuracy
This only happens with older, smaller models

quiz.question: What is 'tool retrieval' as a strategy for scaling tool access?
options: Exposing the entire tool catalog on every single turn
Using a lightweight search step to surface only the tools likely relevant to the current request
Removing tools permanently once the catalog grows too large
A method for compressing tool schemas into fewer bytes

quiz.question: What is the underlying principle connecting tool retrieval, hierarchical routing, and toolset grouping?
options: They all aim to increase the number of visible tools at once
Reducing the visible, irrelevant tool surface for a given request often improves selection accuracy more than refining any single tool's description
They are unrelated strategies with no shared principle
They all require fine-tuning a new model

title: Agent Skills and Composability
content: A 'skill' is a step up from a raw tool: a packaged bundle of instructions, examples, and often one or more underlying tools that together teach an agent how to competently perform a specific, reusable procedure -- like 'draft a customer refund email following our policy' or 'summarize a call transcript into structured notes' -- rather than exposing a single low-level function and hoping the model figures out the right sequence of calls and framing on its own every time. This course covers why skills matter as a design layer: they encode not just what a tool does but how and when to use it well, captured once by an expert and reused reliably across many invocations, instead of re-deriving that judgment from scratch in every prompt. You'll learn about composability -- skills that can invoke other skills, letting you build higher-level capabilities out of lower-level ones, similar to how software functions call other functions -- and the practical challenges this introduces at scale: skill discovery (how does an agent find the right skill among many available), versioning (what happens to agents relying on a skill when that skill's instructions change), and avoiding the same tool-selection confusion that plagues large flat tool lists, just one layer up.

sections.heading: From Function Call to Encoded Judgment: What Makes Something a Skill
sections.body: A raw tool exposes a signature -- send_email(to, subject, body) -- and nothing else. Every time the model calls it, the model itself has to reconstruct the surrounding judgment from scratch: what tone counts as on-policy for a refund, which fields are mandatory versus optional, what to do when the customer is a repeat offender, how to phrase a denial so it doesn't sound like a form letter. A skill takes that judgment -- the part that used to live only in a senior support rep's head -- and packages it once, explicitly, alongside the tool: written instructions ('always cite the specific policy clause'), worked examples of good and bad outputs, edge-case handling ('if the order is over 90 days old, escalate instead of refunding'), and often the underlying tool call itself, bundled together. The distinction matters because it changes where expertise lives. With a bare tool, expertise is re-derived, inconsistently, in every conversation. With a skill, expertise is authored once by someone who knows the domain and then reused verbatim across thousands of invocations -- the same reason a function in software is better than copy-pasting its logic inline every time you need it.

sections.heading: Composability: Higher-Order Skills Built From Lower-Level Ones
sections.body: Once skills exist as discrete, callable units, they compose the same way functions do: a higher-level skill can invoke two or three lower-level skills as steps in its own procedure, rather than reimplementing their logic. Consider a 'handle support ticket' skill. Rather than being one monolithic block of instructions, it's built from three narrower skills: 'classify-ticket-intent' (reads the incoming text and tags it as refund-request, bug-report, or account-question), 'lookup-customer-account' (pulls order history and account standing given an email or order ID), and 'draft-refund-email' (the policy-aware email-writing skill from the earlier section). The composed skill's own instructions are almost entirely orchestration logic: call classify-ticket-intent first; if the tag is refund-request, call lookup-customer-account to check eligibility (order under 90 days, not already refunded); only if both checks pass, call draft-refund-email with the customer's name and order details. Each sub-skill stays independently testable and reusable -- lookup-customer-account gets called by a dozen other skills that have nothing to do with refunds -- while the composed skill adds only the sequencing and branching logic on top. This is exactly the appeal and exactly the risk: the composed skill is now only as reliable as its least reliable dependency, and a bug in classify-ticket-intent silently propagates into every skill built on top of it.

sections.heading: Skill Discovery: Choosing Among Hundreds Instead of a Handful
sections.body: A flat list of 15 tools fits comfortably in a model's context and its own judgment about which to call. A library of 300 skills does not -- and skills tend to proliferate faster than tools because they're cheaper to author (often just a markdown file plus examples, no new API integration required). Discovery is the practical problem this creates: given a user request, how does the agent find the one or two relevant skills out of hundreds without either loading all of their full instructions into context (blowing the token budget) or missing the right one entirely. Production systems typically solve this with a two-tier lookup: a lightweight index -- short name plus one-line description for every skill, cheap enough to keep fully in context or embed for retrieval -- that the agent searches first, followed by loading the full instructions only for the skill(s) that match. This mirrors RAG's retrieve-then-read pattern, and it inherits the same failure modes: two skills with overlapping descriptions ('summarize-call' and 'summarize-transcript') get confused just as easily as two badly-named tools did, just one layer up the stack.

sections.heading: Versioning: When a Skill's Instructions Change Under Its Dependents' Feet
sections.body: A skill is not static -- its author revises the policy language, tightens an edge case, or changes which sub-tools it calls, often without touching its name or its interface. That's fine for direct callers who get the update automatically, but it's a hazard for every higher-level skill that composes it. If 'draft-refund-email' is updated to require a manager-approval step for refunds over $200, the 'handle-support-ticket' skill built on top of it now silently behaves differently -- possibly stalling on tickets that used to complete automatically -- without anyone having touched handle-support-ticket's own code or instructions at all. This is the same dependency-fragility problem software engineering solved with semantic versioning and pinned dependency graphs, and skill systems need an analogous answer: pin composed skills to a specific version of each sub-skill they call, or at minimum log which skill version handled a given invocation so a regression can be traced back to its source. Without that, a behavior change three layers down surfaces as an unexplained shift in a top-level skill's outputs, and debugging it means manually walking the entire call chain because nothing recorded which version ran.

sections.heading: The Confusion Ladder: Tool-Selection Problems Recur One Layer Up
sections.body: It's tempting to think skills solve the tool-selection problem once and for all -- group tools into skills, and the model only has to pick among a handful of skills instead of dozens of raw functions. In practice the same failure modes just move up a level. Two overlapping skills produce the same hesitation and misfires that two overlapping tools did. A skill with a vague description gets invoked for the wrong situations exactly like an under-documented tool does. And a skill that itself composes five sub-skills reintroduces the flat-list problem internally: its own orchestration instructions now have to disambiguate among those five, and if that skill is itself one of 40 skills being chosen from at the top level, the model is effectively navigating two nested decision points instead of one. The fix is the same discipline that worked for tools, applied recursively: keep each skill's scope narrow and its description unambiguous, keep the branching factor at every level low (three to seven options, not thirty), and treat a skill's internal composition as a design problem with its own discovery and clarity requirements -- not a solved problem just because it's wrapped one layer down.

quiz.question: What distinguishes a 'skill' from a raw, low-level tool?
options: A skill is simply a tool renamed for marketing purposes
A skill packages instructions, examples, and often tools together to teach an agent how to competently perform a reusable procedure, not just expose a single function
Skills cannot call any underlying tools
There is no meaningful distinction between the two

quiz.question: What does 'composability' mean in the context of agent skills?
options: Skills can invoke other skills, building higher-level capabilities out of lower-level ones
Skills must always be used in complete isolation from one another
Composability refers only to how skills are stored in a database
Skills cannot be combined under any circumstances

quiz.question: What challenge does skill versioning introduce at scale?
options: Versioning has no practical implications
Agents relying on a skill may behave differently or break when that skill's underlying instructions change
Versioning only matters for raw tools, never for skills
Skills never need to change once created

title: What Is Context Engineering?
content: Context engineering is the discipline of deciding exactly what information goes into a model's context window for a given call -- the system instructions, any retrieved documents, prior conversation history, tool definitions and their outputs, and the current user request -- and in what order and format, so the model has precisely what it needs and nothing that distracts from it. This course frames context engineering as broader than 'prompt engineering': prompt engineering typically focuses on how you word a single instruction, while context engineering is about architecting the whole assembly of information a model sees on every call, especially in systems with retrieval, tools, and multi-turn conversation where the context is dynamically built up rather than a single static prompt someone wrote once. You'll learn why this matters more as systems grow more complex: a simple single-turn Q&A prompt has little to architect, but an agent juggling retrieved documents, a long conversation history, several tool schemas, and evolving task state has a real design problem in deciding what's relevant enough to include, what to summarize, and what to drop, given a fixed and costly context budget.

sections.heading: Prompt Engineering vs. Context Engineering: Where the Line Falls
sections.body: Prompt engineering is about wording: choosing the phrasing, few-shot examples, and instructions that make a single call to the model behave well -- adding 'think step by step,' picking the right verb, giving one clean example of the output format you want. Context engineering sits a level above that. It's the discipline of deciding what goes into the context window at all -- system instructions, retrieved documents, prior turns, tool schemas and their outputs, the current request -- and in what order and format, before any wording decisions even apply. A model with a perfectly worded prompt but the wrong documents retrieved, or a tool output dumped in raw and untruncated, will still fail. Prompt engineering optimizes the words on the page; context engineering decides which pages make it into the book in the first place.

sections.heading: The Five Ingredients That Fill Every Context Window
sections.body: On every call, a model sees some combination of five things: system instructions (the persona and rules that rarely change call to call), retrieved documents (chunks pulled in by a RAG step or search, often 500-2,000 tokens each), conversation history (prior user and assistant turns, which grow unboundedly in a long chat), tool definitions and their outputs (a function's JSON schema plus whatever it returned -- a database query can easily return 10,000 tokens of rows), and the current user request. A model with a 128k-token window might spend 2k on system instructions, 6k on three retrieved chunks, 40k on conversation history, and 15k on a single verbose tool call before the user's actual question is even added. Context engineering is the practice of managing all five deliberately instead of letting them accumulate by default.

sections.heading: Why a Single Q&A Prompt Barely Needs Architecting
sections.body: A one-shot question-answering prompt -- system instruction plus one user question, no history, no tools, no retrieval -- has almost nothing to design: the whole context is a few hundred tokens you wrote once and reused. There's no competition for space and no decision about what to leave out. The problem changes entirely once a system adds retrieval (which chunks, out of hundreds of candidates, actually earn a spot), multi-turn conversation (does turn 40 still need the details from turn 2), and tool use (a dozen tool schemas each costing a few hundred tokens just to describe, whether or not they're used this turn). Complexity in the system is what creates the architecting problem; a static single-turn prompt simply doesn't generate enough inputs to need it.

sections.heading: The Fixed Budget: What's Relevant, What Gets Summarized, What Gets Dropped
sections.body: Context windows are finite and every token in them costs money and latency, so a system with growing inputs -- more retrieved documents, a longer conversation, more available tools -- eventually has to choose. Relevance filtering means ranking retrieved chunks or past turns and keeping only the top handful instead of everything above some similarity threshold. Summarization means compressing turns 1-30 of a conversation into a two-paragraph running summary instead of carrying the full transcript forward verbatim, trading detail for space. Dropping means removing tool definitions the current task doesn't need, or truncating a 10,000-token database result down to the rows that matter. None of these are free: over-aggressive summarization loses a detail the user asks about later, and under-filtering burns budget on irrelevant material that can actually degrade the model's answer, not just its cost.

sections.heading: Position and Format: Content Isn't the Only Thing That Matters
sections.body: Two contexts holding the identical facts can perform differently depending on how those facts are arranged. Models tend to attend more reliably to information near the start and end of a long context and less reliably to material buried in the middle -- a well-documented effect sometimes called 'lost in the middle' -- so where you place the critical instruction or the most relevant retrieved chunk is itself a design decision, not an afterthought. Format matters too: a tool's raw JSON output dropped in unmodified reads differently to the model than the same data reformatted as a short labeled list, and system instructions placed after a long block of retrieved text compete for attention differently than instructions placed first. Context engineering treats ordering and formatting as first-class levers alongside content selection.

quiz.question: How does context engineering differ from narrower 'prompt engineering'?
options: They are exactly the same practice
Context engineering is the broader discipline of architecting everything that goes into the context window, not just wording a single instruction
Prompt engineering only applies to image models
Context engineering only concerns system prompts, nothing else

quiz.question: Why does context engineering become a bigger design problem as systems grow more complex?
options: It doesn't; complexity has no bearing on context design
Systems with retrieval, tools, and long conversations must actively decide what's relevant, what to summarize, and what to drop within a fixed, costly context budget
More complex systems automatically have unlimited context windows
Context engineering only matters for the very first prompt in a conversation

quiz.question: What does context engineering include beyond just the system prompt?
options: Only the system prompt matters; everything else is irrelevant
Retrieved documents, conversation history, tool definitions and outputs, and the current request, in addition to system instructions
Only the user's most recent message
Nothing beyond the model's training data

title: System Prompts vs. User Prompts vs. Conversation History
content: Most chat-based LLM APIs distinguish between a system message (persistent instructions, persona, and constraints that should apply across the whole interaction), user messages (the specific request or question at a given turn), and, over a multi-turn conversation, an accumulating history of prior turns. This course covers how models tend to weight these differently -- system instructions are generally treated as higher-priority framing that should hold even as the conversation continues, while user messages carry the immediate task -- and the common mistake of cramming everything into the system prompt: a system prompt bloated with information that's really turn-specific (like details only relevant to the current question) becomes stale or irrelevant as the conversation moves on, while genuinely persistent rules get buried in a wall of situational detail. You'll learn the practical guideline: put durable behavior rules, persona, and constraints in the system prompt; put the actual task, question, and any turn-specific data in the user message; and let conversation history do the job of carrying forward what's actually been discussed, rather than re-stating it in the system prompt each time.

sections.heading: Three Channels, One Context Window
sections.body: Every chat completion request is actually three separate streams of text stitched together before the model ever sees them: a system message, one or more user messages, and (in a multi-turn conversation) an accumulating history of everything said so far. The API keeps these logically distinct -- each has its own role field -- but under the hood they're concatenated into a single sequence of tokens. The model doesn't experience three inboxes; it experiences one long document with role markers sprinkled through it. That matters because it means the *position* and *labeling* of a piece of text, not just its content, shapes how much weight the model gives it. A rule stated once in the system slot and never repeated still tends to hold 40 turns later, in a way a rule buried in turn 3 of a long user message often doesn't.

sections.heading: Why System Instructions Get Read Differently
sections.body: Models are trained (via instruction tuning and RLHF) to treat the system role as a special, authoritative frame -- closer to 'the rules of the game' than to 'a message in the game.' In practice this means system content is generally weighted as higher-priority and more durable: it's meant to survive the entire conversation, overriding or constraining whatever comes later in user turns. User messages, by contrast, are treated as the live, task-specific ask -- what to do *right now*, given the standing rules. This isn't a hard guarantee (a long enough or repetitive-enough user message can still erode adherence to system instructions, and this is an active area of jailbreak research), but as a working mental model: system = framing that should hold, user = the current task within that framing.

sections.heading: The Overloaded System Prompt Anti-Pattern
sections.body: The most common structural mistake is treating the system prompt as a dumping ground for everything the model might need to know, including details that are really specific to the current turn -- the user's current order number, the specific error message they just pasted, today's date, the one document they're asking about right now. Two things go wrong at once. First, that turn-specific content goes stale the moment the conversation moves to a new topic, but it's still sitting there in every subsequent request, silently misleading the model. Second, genuinely durable rules -- 'always cite sources,' 'never give medical advice,' 'respond in the user's language' -- get buried under paragraphs of situational detail, diluting the very instructions the system prompt exists to protect. A 2,000-token system prompt where only 200 tokens are actually persistent is a 200-token system prompt with 1,800 tokens of noise.

sections.heading: A Practical Split: Durable Rules vs. Turn-Specific Data
sections.body: The fix is a simple sorting test applied to every piece of information before it goes anywhere: would this still be true and relevant in turn 20 of this conversation? If yes -- persona, tone, output format, safety constraints, domain scope, tool-use policy -- it belongs in the system prompt, written once. If no -- the customer's specific question, the file they just uploaded, a number they just gave you -- it belongs in the user message for that turn, and only that turn. A support bot's system prompt should say 'you are a calm, concise support agent for Acme Cloud; never promise refunds without escalation'; it should not say 'the customer's order #48213 shipped on Tuesday and is currently delayed' -- that's user-message material, true for exactly one conversation.

sections.heading: Letting History Do Its Job
sections.body: Conversation history exists precisely so you don't have to keep re-stating what's already been established -- it's the model's memory of the interaction, and re-injecting old facts into the system prompt on every turn is redundant at best and contradictory at worst if the system prompt and the actual history ever drift apart. If a user told the model their name, their preferred language, or the topic of discussion three turns ago, that's already present in the accumulated messages; trust it, rather than trying to hoist it into a 'persistent' system prompt that now has to be regenerated and kept in sync every single turn. The practical guideline that ties this course together: system prompt for rules that don't change, user message for what's being asked right now, history for everything that's already been said.

quiz.question: What is a common mistake when structuring system prompts?
options: Keeping them too short
Cramming turn-specific information into the system prompt, where it becomes stale and buries genuinely persistent rules
Never including any instructions at all
Only using system prompts for single-turn conversations

quiz.question: What content is best suited for the system prompt versus the user message?
options: Everything belongs in the system prompt regardless of type
Durable behavior rules, persona, and constraints belong in the system prompt; the actual task and turn-specific data belong in the user message
The user message should contain the persona and constraints
There's no meaningful distinction between the two message types

quiz.question: How do models generally treat system instructions relative to user messages over a conversation?
options: System instructions are ignored after the first turn
System instructions are generally treated as higher-priority framing that should hold throughout the conversation
User messages always override system instructions completely
There's no difference in how either is weighted

title: Context Window Budgeting
content: Every token in a model's context window costs money and competes for the model's limited attention, so treating the context window as a scarce, deliberately allocated budget -- rather than an unlimited scratchpad -- is a core context engineering skill. This course covers how to think about allocating that budget across competing needs: system instructions and tool schemas (often fixed, paid on every call), retrieved knowledge (variable, should scale with how much evidence the query genuinely needs, not a fixed chunk count regardless of question complexity), conversation history (grows unboundedly over a long session unless actively managed), and headroom for the model's own output. You'll learn practical budgeting techniques: setting explicit token caps per section, truncating or summarizing the oldest conversation turns once a threshold is hit rather than letting history grow unchecked, and dynamically adjusting how many retrieved chunks to include based on a relevance-score cutoff rather than always including a fixed top-k regardless of how relevant they actually are. The core skill this course builds: recognizing when a system's cost or quality problems trace back to poor context budgeting -- too much irrelevant history, too many low-relevance retrieved chunks -- rather than the underlying model being inadequate.

sections.heading: Treating the Context Window as a Line-Item Budget, Not a Scratchpad
sections.body: The instinct to just stuff everything relevant into the prompt breaks down for two concrete reasons: cost and attention. Cost is straightforward -- if you're paying $3 per million input tokens and your system prompt plus tool schemas run 2,000 tokens on every single call across 50,000 calls a day, that's real money burned on fixed overhead before a single user question is answered. Attention is subtler but matters more for quality: models don't weigh every token in the context window equally. Research on long-context recall (the 'lost in the middle' effect) shows retrieval accuracy for information placed in the middle of a long context can drop noticeably compared to information near the start or end. So a context window stuffed to 80% capacity with marginally-relevant material doesn't just cost more -- it can actively degrade the model's ability to find and use the one paragraph that actually answers the question. Budgeting means assigning each category of content -- system instructions, tool schemas, retrieved knowledge, conversation history, output headroom -- an explicit allocation you track and enforce, not a hope that it all fits.

sections.heading: Setting Explicit Token Caps Per Section
sections.body: A practical budget starts with a hard ceiling per section, enforced with a tokenizer (e.g. tiktoken for OpenAI-family models, or the target model's own counting endpoint), not a word-count guess. A common allocation for a 128k-token window: system instructions and tool schemas capped at 3-4k tokens (these are fixed costs paid every call, so trim tool descriptions and avoid redundant schema fields aggressively); retrieved context capped at a variable ceiling like 20-40% of the window depending on task; conversation history capped at roughly 20-30%; and 15-25% reserved as output headroom so the model isn't cut off mid-answer. When a section's content exceeds its cap, you need a deterministic policy for what gets cut -- truncate from the oldest end, drop the lowest-scoring retrieved chunks, or summarize rather than silently overflow into another section's allocation. Caps also serve as an early-warning system: if tool schemas alone are eating 8k tokens, that's a signal to prune the toolset before you ever touch the harder problems of history and retrieval.

sections.heading: Managing Conversation History: Truncation vs. Summarization
sections.body: Left unmanaged, conversation history grows linearly with turn count and will eventually crowd out every other section -- this is the single most common cause of a system that gets slower and worse the longer a session runs. Two techniques handle it, and they trade off differently. Truncation (sliding window) keeps only the most recent N turns or the most recent T tokens, dropping everything older once a threshold is hit -- cheap and fast, but loses information a user referenced early in a long session ('remember when I said my budget was $5k'). Summarization periodically compresses older turns into a condensed summary (e.g. every 10 turns, replace the oldest 10 with a 200-token summary generated by a cheap model call), preserving gist at the cost of an extra LLM call and some fidelity loss. Production systems often combine both: keep the last 3-5 turns verbatim for coherence, summarize the middle, and drop or archive the earliest turns entirely. The threshold that triggers either action should be a token count, not a turn count -- a single turn with a large pasted document can blow the budget faster than ten short back-and-forth exchanges.

sections.heading: Relevance-Cutoff Retrieval Instead of Fixed Top-K
sections.body: Always fetching the same top-k (say, top-5) retrieved chunks regardless of the question is a common default, and it's wrong in both directions. A simple factual question ('what's our refund window?') might be fully answered by one high-scoring chunk -- including four more at similarity scores of 0.4-0.5 just burns budget on noise and adds lost-in-the-middle risk. Conversely, a genuinely complex multi-part question might need eight or ten chunks to cover all its sub-claims, and a fixed top-5 silently omits the evidence needed for the last two parts, producing a confidently incomplete answer. A relevance-cutoff approach instead sets a similarity-score threshold (e.g. cosine similarity above 0.75, or a cross-encoder reranker score above a calibrated bar) and includes every chunk that clears it, up to a token ceiling as a backstop -- so the number of chunks included varies naturally with how much genuine evidence the query needs. This requires your retrieval scores to be well-calibrated (raw embedding similarity is often noisier than a reranker's score), but it converts retrieval from a fixed cost into a budget that scales with actual query difficulty.

sections.heading: Diagnosing Budget Problems vs. Model Problems
sections.body: When a system's answers degrade, the reflexive move is to blame the model -- swap in a bigger one, add more few-shot examples, write a longer system prompt. Before doing any of that, check whether the real cause is budget mismanagement, because the symptoms look similar but the fixes are opposite. Two diagnostic patterns to check first: if quality drops and latency creeps up specifically as conversation length increases, unbounded history accumulation is the prime suspect -- instrument token counts per section per call and watch history's share grow over a session. If quality is inconsistent across queries of different complexity -- great on simple questions, weak on ones needing broad evidence -- a fixed top-k retrieval policy starving complex queries of context (or drowning simple ones in irrelevant chunks) is the likely culprit, not the model's reasoning ability. The tell in both cases is the same: adding a bigger, more capable model doesn't fix it, because the model isn't the bottleneck -- what's actually in its context window is.

quiz.question: Why should context window allocation be treated as a deliberate budget rather than an unlimited scratchpad?
options: Context windows are free and unlimited in practice
Every token costs money and competes for the model's limited attention, so allocation choices directly affect cost and quality
Budgeting only matters for image-based models
There is no cost associated with context length

quiz.question: Why is always including a fixed top-k number of retrieved chunks, regardless of relevance, a weaker approach than a relevance-score cutoff?
options: Fixed top-k is always the better approach
It can include low-relevance chunks that waste budget on queries needing little evidence, or omit needed evidence on queries needing more
Relevance scores are never available in retrieval systems
Chunk count has no effect on context budget

quiz.question: A system's answers are getting worse and slower as conversations get longer. What is a likely context-budgeting culprit?
options: The model has stopped working entirely
Unbounded conversation history is accumulating and crowding out budget for more relevant content
This can only be caused by a change in the underlying model
Longer conversations always improve answer quality with no downside

title: Memory and State Management for Conversational Agents
content: Conversational agents need to track two different kinds of memory: short-term memory, the state relevant to the current session (what's been discussed in this conversation so far), and long-term memory, information that should persist and be recalled across separate sessions (a user's stated preferences, past decisions, ongoing project context). This course covers common techniques for each: a sliding window that keeps only the most recent N turns in context, summarization buffers that periodically condense older turns into a compact summary rather than dropping them entirely, and external memory stores (often a simple database or a vector store) that hold long-term facts the agent can retrieve when relevant, rather than trying to keep everything in the live context window indefinitely. You'll learn a real risk with long-term memory that's easy to overlook: stale or incorrect information persisting across sessions can actively mislead an agent later -- if a user's preference or a fact changes and the memory store isn't updated or invalidated, the agent may confidently apply outdated information in a later session, which can be harder to detect and debug than a single-session context problem because the wrong information didn't even originate in the current conversation.

sections.heading: Two Tiers of Memory: Session State vs. Persistent Store
sections.body: Every conversational agent has to answer the same architectural question twice: what needs to survive to the next turn, and what needs to survive to the next session. Short-term memory is the state relevant to the current conversation -- the running transcript, tool outputs, any scratch variables the agent set for itself -- and it typically lives directly in the context window or a session object that's discarded when the conversation ends. Long-term memory is different in kind, not just duration: it's information deliberately written out of the live conversation into a separate store (a database row, a vector index entry, a key-value cache) so that a future session, potentially days or months later and with an empty context window, can retrieve it. A user saying 'I prefer Python over JS' in March should still shape an agent's answers in August, even though March's context window is long gone. Conflating the two tiers is a common design mistake: treating everything as short-term means long-term facts get silently lost when the session ends, while treating everything as long-term means you're paying retrieval and storage overhead for state that only ever mattered for the next three turns.

sections.heading: The Sliding Window: Bounding Context by Turn Count
sections.body: The sliding window is the simplest short-term memory technique: keep only the most recent N turns (or the most recent N tokens) in the context sent to the model, and drop everything older. Implementation is trivial -- a deque with a max length, or a token-counting loop that pops the oldest message once you exceed a budget like 8,000 tokens -- which is exactly why it's the default in most agent frameworks. The tradeoff is equally blunt: information isn't summarized or archived, it's discarded outright. If a user mentioned a critical constraint in turn 2 and the window only holds the last 10 turns, by turn 13 that constraint is gone from the model's view entirely, and the agent will contradict itself with no visibility into why. This makes sliding windows well-suited to short, transactional exchanges (a quick lookup, a single-turn code fix) and poorly suited to long, exploratory sessions where early context stays load-bearing -- a multi-hour debugging session where the original error message needs to stay in view is the canonical failure case.

sections.heading: Summarization Buffers: Compressing Instead of Discarding
sections.body: A summarization buffer solves the sliding window's core weakness -- outright loss -- by periodically condensing older turns into a compact summary rather than dropping them. The typical pattern: once the raw transcript exceeds a threshold (say, 15 turns or 6,000 tokens), the oldest chunk is sent to the model (often the same model, sometimes a cheaper one) with a prompt like 'summarize the key facts, decisions, and open questions from this exchange in under 200 words,' and that summary permanently replaces the raw turns at the front of the context. As the conversation continues, the summary itself gets periodically re-summarized alongside new content, so it stays roughly constant in size even as the underlying conversation grows unbounded. This preserves some information as context grows, at the cost of fidelity: a summary necessarily loses verbatim detail (exact numbers, exact phrasing, code snippets), so summarization buffers work best for narrative or decision-tracking content and worst for anything where the agent needs to quote or reference precise values it saw earlier. Latency and cost are real considerations too -- each summarization pass is itself an LLM call.

sections.heading: External Memory Stores: Retrieval Over Retention
sections.body: Long-term memory is usually implemented as an external store the agent queries rather than a window it keeps in context. Two common shapes dominate: a structured store (a SQL table or key-value store keyed by user ID, holding fields like stated preferences, past decisions, or project metadata) for facts you'll look up by exact key, and a vector store for facts you'll retrieve by semantic similarity -- past conversation summaries or notes embedded and indexed, so a new session's opening message can be used to query for 'anything relevant to this' before the agent responds. The architectural shift this represents is important: instead of trying to keep everything live in an ever-growing context window, the agent writes facts out during a session (often via an explicit tool call like `save_memory(fact)`) and reads them back selectively at the start of a new session or when a retrieval query matches. This keeps the live context small and focused, but it introduces a new failure surface: retrieval quality. If the write step never captures a fact, or the read step's query doesn't semantically match how the fact was stored, the agent behaves as if it never learned it at all.

sections.heading: The Staleness Trap: When Persisted Facts Go Wrong
sections.body: External memory stores introduce a failure mode that single-session context problems don't have: the information can be wrong not because the model misread something, but because the world changed after the fact was written and nothing updated the store. A user tells the agent in January 'I'm using Postgres for this project,' the agent writes that to long-term memory, and by June the team has migrated to a different database -- but if no session ever explicitly corrects or invalidates that stored fact, the agent will keep confidently recommending Postgres-specific solutions months later. This is meaningfully harder to detect and debug than a sliding-window or summarization error: those errors originate visibly in the current conversation, where a user can immediately notice the agent contradicting something just said. A stale long-term memory error originates in a past session the current user may not even remember, so the incorrect behavior looks like an unprompted, unexplainable mistake rather than an obvious consequence of a specific input. Mitigations include timestamping stored facts, expiring or re-confirming them periodically, and explicit invalidation calls when a user states something that contradicts a stored fact -- but none of this happens automatically unless the system is designed for it.

options: There is no meaningful difference
Short-term memory covers the current session's state; long-term memory persists and is recalled across separate sessions
Long-term memory only applies to a single conversation turn
Short-term memory is always stored in a vector database

quiz.question: What is a real risk of long-term memory stores that's easy to overlook?
options: Long-term memory has no risks at all
Stale or incorrect information can persist across sessions and mislead the agent later, in a way that's hard to trace back to its origin
Long-term memory always self-corrects automatically
Long-term memory can only ever improve agent performance

quiz.question: What does a summarization buffer do that a plain sliding window doesn't?
options: It discards all older turns with no trace
It condenses older turns into a compact summary rather than dropping them entirely, preserving some information as context grows
It has an identical effect to a sliding window
It only applies to system prompts

title: Context Compression Techniques
content: As conversations, retrieved evidence, and tool outputs accumulate, keeping every raw token in context becomes expensive and eventually infeasible, so this course covers techniques for compressing context while preserving what actually matters. Summarizing older turns condenses a long transcript into a shorter representation of what was discussed, trading some nuance and exact wording for a large reduction in token count. Extracting structured facts goes further, pulling out just the specific data points a later step will need (like a set of key-value facts established earlier in the conversation) rather than keeping a prose summary at all, which is often more reliable for information a downstream step needs to use precisely. Prompt caching, offered by several providers, lets you avoid recomputing and re-paying for a stable prefix (like a long system prompt or a set of few-shot examples) across repeated calls, which isn't compression in the traditional sense but achieves a similar practical goal of not re-processing the same context repeatedly. You'll learn the central tradeoff underlying all compression: the more aggressively you compress, the more you risk losing a specific detail that turns out to matter later, so compression decisions should be informed by what a task is likely to need, not applied uniformly regardless of context.

sections.heading: Why Raw Context Accumulation Breaks Down
sections.body: Every additional turn, retrieved document, or tool call result you keep verbatim adds tokens that must be re-sent and re-processed on every subsequent model call -- not just stored once. A long-running agent session that starts at 2,000 tokens can easily reach 150,000+ tokens after a few dozen tool calls, and most production context windows (128K-200K tokens for common models, sometimes more) get consumed faster than people expect once tool outputs -- stack traces, API responses, full file contents -- start piling up alongside conversation turns. The costs are threefold: dollar cost (you pay per input token, every call, even for tokens the model doesn't need), latency (time-to-first-token scales with prompt length), and attention degradation (models demonstrably attend less reliably to details buried in the middle of very long contexts, a well-documented 'lost in the middle' effect). Compression exists to push back on all three, but the mechanism you choose changes what information survives -- so the rest of this course treats summarization, structured extraction, and prompt caching as distinct tools with different failure modes, not interchangeable ways to 'shrink the prompt.'

sections.heading: Summarization: Trading Wording for Token Count
sections.body: Summarization asks the model to re-express a stretch of transcript -- often the oldest N turns, or everything before the most recent 'active window' -- as a shorter paragraph or a few bullet points, then discards the originals. A common pattern is rolling summarization: each time the transcript crosses a length threshold, the oldest chunk gets folded into (and replaces) the running summary, so the summary itself compounds over the session rather than being regenerated from scratch. Hierarchical summarization goes further, summarizing summaries at multiple levels for very long sessions (a day's worth of agent activity, say), trading progressively more detail for a bounded token footprint. The failure mode is paraphrase drift: a summary of 'the user said the deploy window is 2am-4am PT on Tuesdays, and the rollback owner is Priya' easily degrades to 'discussed deployment scheduling and ownership' -- technically accurate, operationally useless if a later step needs the actual time window or the name. Summarization is well-suited to narrative context (what was the user trying to accomplish, what's the emotional tenor of a support thread) and poorly suited to anything a downstream step will need to act on precisely.

sections.heading: Structured Fact Extraction: Precision Instead of Narrative
sections.body: Structured extraction skips prose entirely: instead of summarizing turns, you prompt the model (often via a tool-use/function-calling schema, or plain JSON mode) to pull out a fixed set of fields -- {"budget": "$47,500", "deploy_window": "Tue 02:00-04:00 PT", "rollback_owner": "Priya Nair"} -- from the accumulated conversation, then carry forward just that structured record instead of a summary of the discussion that produced it. This is more reliable than summarization for anything a downstream step consumes programmatically or needs verbatim, for two concrete reasons: a schema forces the model to commit to a specific value per field rather than letting a number get softened into a description during paraphrase, and validation becomes possible (you can check the extracted budget parses as currency, the date is well-formed) in a way that free-text summary output never allows. The tradeoff is coverage: a schema only captures what you thought to ask for in advance, so anything outside the predefined fields is silently dropped, whereas a summary -- however imprecise -- at least gestures at everything discussed. Mature systems often run both: a structured extraction pass for the handful of facts a task is known to need, plus a lighter summary for everything else, updated incrementally as new turns arrive rather than re-derived from the full transcript each time.

sections.heading: Prompt Caching: Avoiding Reprocessing Without Compressing
sections.body: Prompt caching doesn't shrink what you send -- it lets the provider skip recomputing the attention/KV-cache state for a prefix it has already processed on a prior call, as long as that prefix is byte-identical and within a time-to-live window. Anthropic's implementation uses explicit cache_control breakpoints in the request (you mark where the stable prefix ends -- a long system prompt, tool definitions, a set of few-shot examples, or a large document you'll query repeatedly), with a minimum cacheable segment of 1024 tokens for Claude and a default 5-minute TTL (extendable to 1 hour on supported models); cache writes cost roughly 1.25x the base input price but cache reads cost around a tenth of it, so the economics favor any prefix you'll reuse across even a handful of calls. OpenAI's automatic prompt caching works similarly but requires no explicit markers -- prefixes over 1024 tokens are cached transparently. The reason this belongs in a compression course despite not reducing token count: it achieves the same practical goal (not re-paying, in latency and dollars, to reprocess context you've already shown the model) through a completely different mechanism, and it composes with true compression -- you might cache a large stable system prompt while summarizing the volatile conversation tail sitting after it.

sections.heading: The Central Tradeoff: Compression Should Be Task-Informed, Not Uniform
sections.body: Every compression technique trades fidelity for token count, and the risk compounds silently: a detail dropped during summarization, or a field never captured because it wasn't in your extraction schema, doesn't announce itself as missing -- it just isn't there when a later step needs it, often many turns after the compression happened, which makes root-causing failures on aggressively compressed pipelines genuinely hard. The discipline this demands is asking, before compressing, what the remaining task actually needs: an agent whose job is to maintain rapport and tone across a long support conversation can tolerate heavy summarization of earlier turns, but an agent that will later need to file an exact expense amount or quote a specific clause back to the user needs that value preserved structurally, not paraphrased. In practice this means auditing your compression points against your task's known information needs -- what facts will definitely be needed downstream, what's merely helpful color -- rather than applying one compression ratio or one technique uniformly across an entire pipeline. The mature pattern layers techniques: cache the stable, reused prefix; extract the small set of facts you know later steps depend on; summarize everything else; and revisit that split whenever the downstream task's requirements change, because a compression scheme tuned for one task can silently fail a different one reusing the same context.

title: Multi-Turn Context Drift and the 'Lost in the Middle' Effect
content: Long conversations and long contexts don't just cost more -- they can measurably degrade an agent's behavior, a phenomenon this course covers under two related ideas. Context drift describes how, over many turns, a conversation can accumulate noise, tangents, and even outright contradictions (a user changes their mind, or an earlier assumption turns out to be wrong), and if the agent keeps weighing everything in the accumulated history equally, its behavior can drift away from the current, correct state of the task. The 'lost in the middle' effect describes a documented tendency for models to attend more reliably to information near the beginning and end of a long context than to content buried in the middle, meaning a critical instruction or fact placed in the middle of a very long prompt can be effectively under-weighted even though it's technically present. You'll learn practical mitigations for both: periodically re-injecting key instructions or the current, corrected state near the end of the context (closer to where the model is about to generate) rather than relying on something stated many turns ago, and actively pruning or correcting outdated information from history instead of letting contradictions accumulate silently.

sections.heading: Context Drift Is Not a Positional Problem -- It's a Semantic One
sections.body: It's tempting to treat context drift as just another flavor of 'lost in the middle,' but the two are mechanically different failure modes and conflating them leads to the wrong fix. Positional effects are about where a token sits in the window. Drift is about what happens when a conversation accumulates content that semantically contradicts itself, regardless of position. A transformer has no built-in 'supersede' operation -- there's no token that means 'ignore turn 4, it's been overruled.' Every prior turn is just more tokens in the same undifferentiated sequence, and the model has to infer, purely from surface cues like recency and phrasing, which of two conflicting statements is the one to trust. It usually does this imperfectly. Researchers at Microsoft and Salesforce (Laban et al., 'LLMs Get Lost in Multi-Turn Conversation,' 2025) found an average 39% performance drop across six generation tasks when the same instructions were revealed incrementally across turns instead of given fully-specified up front -- direct evidence that drift degrades output quality independent of any positional attention bias.

sections.heading: Premature Commitment: Why Agents Double Down on Retracted Assumptions
sections.body: The dominant mechanism behind drift is what the multi-turn literature calls premature commitment: a model forms an interpretation of the task early, often from an ambiguous or incomplete first turn, and generates output consistent with that interpretation. When a later turn corrects or contradicts it, the model doesn't cleanly discard the old interpretation -- it tends to average, hedge between, or partially retain it, because both the original framing and the correction are sitting in context with roughly equal claim on the model's attention. A concrete example: a user asks for 'a script to process this data' (turn 1), the agent assumes Python and starts sketching pandas code, then the user says 'actually, this needs to run in a browser, so JavaScript' (turn 6). Ten turns later, agent-generated code still leaks Pythonic idioms (list comprehensions rendered as odd JS, snake_case variables) because the original framing was never actively retracted, only outweighed. In agentic contexts specifically, tool output staleness compounds this: a file read at turn 3 is cached in context as 'the current file contents,' and if the agent doesn't re-read after edits at turn 15, it reasons over a stale snapshot with the same confidence as fresh observations.

sections.heading: The 'Lost in the Middle' U-Curve: Positional Attention Decay
sections.body: Where drift is about contradictory content, 'lost in the middle' is purely about position: a well-documented tendency (Liu et al., 'Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts,' 2023) for retrieval and reasoning accuracy to trace a U-shaped curve across a long context -- strong near the start, strong near the end, and measurably worse for content buried in between. In their multi-document QA benchmark, placing the answer-bearing document at position 1 or position 20 (of 20) produced meaningfully higher accuracy than placing it at position 10, with drops of 20+ percentage points in some configurations, even though the model technically had access to the same information either way. The mechanism is a combination of training distribution (system instructions and task framing overwhelmingly appear at the start of training examples, teaching a primacy bias) and positional encoding schemes like RoPE, whose relative-distance-based attenuation makes far-apart token pairs harder to attend to strongly. Critically, this effect gets worse, not better, as context windows grow to 200K-1M+ tokens: a bigger window just means a bigger middle for a critical instruction to get lost in.

sections.heading: Mitigation: Recency-Anchored Re-Injection of Current State
sections.body: The most reliable fix for both phenomena, but especially for 'lost in the middle,' is to stop fighting positional bias and start exploiting it: instead of trusting that an instruction stated at turn 3 will still carry weight at turn 40, periodically re-inject the current, corrected state of the task as close as possible to the point where the model is about to generate -- typically appended just before the final user turn, not buried mid-context. A practical pattern is a 'current state' block, refreshed every few turns, explicitly labeled to signal authority: 'CURRENT STATE (supersedes anything stated earlier): target language is JavaScript, output format is JSON, file X was last edited at turn 15.' This does double duty -- it defeats positional attention decay by exploiting recency bias, and it defeats drift by giving the model a single unambiguous source of truth to weigh against a haystack of possibly-contradicted earlier turns, rather than making it adjudicate between N scattered statements on its own.

sections.heading: Mitigation: Actively Pruning History Instead of Letting It Accumulate
sections.body: Re-injection helps the model find the right answer even when contradictions are present, but the more durable fix for drift is to stop the contradictions from accumulating in the first place. This means treating conversation history as an editable working-memory structure rather than an append-only log: periodic summarization compaction that collapses N raw turns into a state summary and drops the originals, diffing new tool output against what's cached and replacing stale entries rather than appending new ones alongside them, and explicitly tagging superseded statements when they can't be removed outright. The judgment call is knowing when to prune versus preserve: aggressive summarization risks discarding a nuance or caveat that later reasoning actually needed, so pruning is the right call when the cost of a lingering contradiction (an agent silently reverting to a retracted assumption) outweighs the cost of losing fine detail -- generally true for state like file paths, format choices, and user decisions -- and the wrong call for exploratory or creative work where preserving the full texture of earlier reasoning is itself valuable.

content: This capstone validates practical context engineering judgment: architecting what goes into a model's context, budgeting a limited context window across competing needs, managing memory across sessions, and recognizing degradation from context drift or the 'lost in the middle' effect. title: How Token Pricing Works
content: Most LLM providers price API usage per token, typically quoted as a rate per one million tokens, and understanding this billing unit is the foundation for every cost decision that follows. This course covers the basic calculation: total cost for a request equals input tokens processed times the input rate, plus output tokens generated times the output rate, and these two rates are usually different from each other. You'll walk through a concrete example: if a provider charges $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, a request with a 2,000-token prompt and a 500-token response costs roughly (2,000 / 1,000,000 x $3) + (500 / 1,000,000 x $15) -- about $0.006 for input plus $0.0075 for output, around $0.0135 total, which sounds trivial per call but adds up quickly at scale: a feature serving 100,000 requests a day at that rate is already over $1,300 a day. You'll learn why teams need to estimate token counts before shipping a feature, not just track spend after the fact, since a seemingly small per-request cost can become a large recurring expense once multiplied by real usage volume.

sections.heading: Tokens as the Billing Unit -- Why Not Characters or Words?
sections.body: LLM providers don't bill by the character or the word -- they bill by the token, the actual unit the model's tokenizer breaks text into. A tokenizer like OpenAI's tiktoken (BPE-based) or Anthropic's equivalent splits text into subword pieces: common English words often map to a single token, rarer words split into two or three, and as a rough rule of thumb one token averages about 4 characters or roughly 0.75 words. This matters practically -- "tokenization" itself might be two tokens, while "the" is one. Non-English text, code, and unusual formatting (JSON with lots of punctuation, for example) tend to tokenize less efficiently, sometimes 1.5-2x more tokens per character than plain English prose. Providers quote rates per one million tokens (e.g., "$3 / 1M input tokens") precisely because token count, not character count, is what determines the compute the model actually does -- and therefore what the provider charges you for.

sections.heading: The Cost Formula: Input Rate Plus Output Rate
sections.body: Every request's cost breaks into exactly two terms: (input tokens x input rate) + (output tokens x output rate). These are tracked and billed separately because a single API call consumes both -- the tokens you send in the prompt and the tokens the model generates in response -- and providers meter them independently. Take a provider charging $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens: a request with a 2,000-token prompt and a 500-token response costs (2,000 / 1,000,000 x $3) = $0.006 for input, plus (500 / 1,000,000 x $15) = $0.0075 for output, for a total of $0.0135. Note the output half is more than half the total cost despite being a quarter of the token count -- that asymmetry in rate, not just volume, is why teams model the two terms separately rather than treating "tokens" as one undifferentiated cost bucket.

sections.heading: Why Output Tokens Cost More Than Input Tokens
sections.body: Input and output rates differ -- often by 3x to 5x, sometimes more -- because the two operations aren't computationally equivalent. Processing input tokens is largely parallelizable: the model can ingest and encode the entire prompt in one forward pass, and providers can batch many requests' prompts together efficiently, plus cache repeated prefixes (system prompts, few-shot examples) to avoid recomputing them. Generating output tokens is autoregressive -- the model produces one token, feeds it back in, produces the next, one at a time, sequentially, which is far harder to parallelize and batch across requests. That sequential dependency means generation consumes more GPU time per token than encoding does. Providers pass that cost difference straight through: input tokens are priced as "reading" cost, output tokens as "writing" cost, and the higher output rate is a direct reflection of the heavier, less parallelizable compute generation requires.

sections.heading: From Per-Call Pennies to Per-Day Line Items
sections.body: A $0.0135 request looks negligible in isolation -- it's the kind of number that's easy to wave away in a design review. But cost per call is only half the picture; the other half is call volume, and production features rarely stay small. At 100,000 requests a day, that same $0.0135 becomes $1,350 a day, or roughly $40,000 a month, and $480,000+ annualized -- all from a single feature at a single usage tier, before any traffic growth. The arithmetic is linear and unforgiving: doubling daily active users doubles the bill, adding a second LLM call per request (a re-ranking step, a verification pass) roughly doubles it again. Costs that look trivial at prototype scale (a few dozen test calls) and costs that look alarming at production scale (hundreds of thousands of calls) are the exact same per-token rate -- only the multiplier changed.

sections.heading: Estimating Before You Ship, Not Just Tracking After
sections.body: Because the per-request cost multiplies directly into a recurring expense, the right time to compute it is during design, not after the invoice arrives. Before shipping, estimate: average prompt length in tokens (system prompt + retrieved context + user input, if any), expected output length, and projected daily call volume -- then run the same formula used for a single request across that volume to get a daily and monthly figure. This catches problems a post-hoc spend dashboard catches too late: a verbose system prompt repeated on every call, an output length that balloons past what the feature needs, or a call pattern (looping, retries, chained sub-calls) that silently multiplies token usage per user action. Estimating ahead turns a possible end-of-month surprise into a known, budgeted number, and gives you the chance to redesign -- shorter prompts, capped output length, caching -- before the cost is already locked in at scale.

title: Input vs. Output Token Costs: Why They Differ
content: Across most providers, output tokens cost noticeably more per token than input tokens, often several times as much, and this course explains why that asymmetry exists and what it implies for how you design a system. Processing input tokens (the 'prefill' stage) can largely happen in parallel -- the model can process the entire prompt's tokens together in one pass. Generating output tokens happens autoregressively, one token at a time, where each new token depends on all the previous ones, making generation inherently more sequential and computationally expensive per token. You'll learn the practical design implication: a verbose system that generates long explanations, extensive reasoning traces, or repeats large amounts of input back in its output pays a disproportionate cost penalty compared to a system that's equally accurate but concise, and instructing a model to be appropriately brief (or asking for a structured, compact output format like a short JSON object instead of a long prose explanation) can meaningfully reduce cost without meaningfully reducing quality, in tasks where verbosity wasn't actually adding value.

sections.heading: Two Different Compute Patterns: Prefill vs. Decode
sections.body: Every LLM request runs through two phases with fundamentally different performance characteristics. The first, prefill, happens when the model reads your prompt: all of the input tokens -- whether it's 50 or 50,000 -- get pushed through the transformer's layers in a single forward pass. Each token's attention computation can be done alongside every other token's, because the full sequence is already sitting in memory before generation starts. This makes prefill embarrassingly parallel: it's dominated by large matrix multiplications that GPUs are extremely good at saturating, so throughput scales well even as prompts grow long. The second phase, decode (generation), works completely differently. The model produces exactly one output token, appends it to the sequence, then must run another full forward pass to produce the next one -- and it can't skip ahead or batch across positions within a single response, because token N+1's computation depends on having already produced token N. That structural difference, not some arbitrary business decision, is the root cause of the price gap you see in every provider's rate card.

sections.heading: Why Sequential Generation Costs More Per Token
sections.body: Decode is what's called memory-bandwidth-bound rather than compute-bound. To generate a single token, the GPU has to load the entire model's weights (and the growing key-value cache of every prior token) from memory, run one comparatively tiny matrix-vector operation, then throw most of that loaded data away and reload nearly the same amount to produce the very next token. On modern hardware, moving data is slower than doing arithmetic on it, so the GPU spends most of its cycles waiting on memory transfers rather than computing -- utilization during decode commonly sits in the 10-20% range, versus 50-70%+ during prefill. Techniques like continuous batching (interleaving decode steps from many concurrent requests) claw back some of that waste, but they can't eliminate the underlying constraint: a 500-token response requires 500 sequential round-trips through the model, each one paying the same fixed memory-bandwidth tax, while a 500-token prompt pays that tax roughly once. That per-token inefficiency is what providers pass through as a several-times-higher output rate -- commonly 3x to 5x the input price, sometimes more for reasoning-heavy models.

sections.heading: Reading the Rate Cards: What the Ratio Actually Reflects
sections.body: When you compare provider pricing pages, the input/output split isn't marketing -- it's a fairly direct readout of the prefill/decode cost asymmetry described above. A frontier model might list $3 per million input tokens against $15 per million output tokens, a 5x ratio; a smaller, cheaper model might show $0.15 versus $0.60, the same 4x shape at a different scale. The ratio tends to widen further for models built around extended reasoning, where a large internal 'thinking' trace is generated token-by-token before the visible answer even starts -- all of that hidden reasoning bills as output tokens at the output rate, even though the user never reads it. This is why two requests with identical prompts and identical final answers can have wildly different bills: the one that reasoned through 2,000 internal tokens before answering pays for all 2,000 at the expensive rate, while a more direct model answering the same question might generate a fraction of that.

sections.heading: The Verbosity Tax: When Chatty Output Quietly Inflates Your Bill
sections.body: Because output tokens are the expensive side of the ledger, any habit that inflates output length -- without adding value -- becomes a direct and often invisible cost multiplier. Common offenders: a system prompt that never asks for a length constraint, so the model defaults to a few paragraphs of hedged prose where three bullet points would answer the question; a summarization task that echoes large chunks of the source text back verbatim inside the 'summary'; or a classification task where the model explains its reasoning in full sentences before finally stating the one-word label you actually needed. None of these make the answer more correct. They just mean you're paying the 3-5x output rate on tokens that a tighter prompt or format would have eliminated. At scale -- thousands or millions of requests a day -- a system that generates 400 output tokens per call versus one generating 120 tokens for equivalent quality isn't a rounding error, it's a multiple-of-the-total-bill difference.

sections.heading: Designing for Brevity: Concrete Ways to Cut Output Cost
sections.body: The fix flows directly from the mechanism: since every unnecessary output token is billed at the expensive decode rate, trimming output length without hurting quality is one of the highest-leverage cost levers available, and it costs nothing to try. Concrete tactics: explicitly instruct the model on desired length or format ('respond in one sentence,' 'return only the JSON object, no explanation'); request structured output (a compact JSON schema) instead of free-form prose whenever a downstream system will parse the answer anyway, since structured fields are almost always shorter than the equivalent explanation; and for reasoning-capable models, set or lower the reasoning-effort/thinking-budget parameter when the task doesn't actually need extended deliberation, since that hidden reasoning bills at full output price. None of this touches input cost or model choice -- it's purely about not paying for verbosity the task never needed, which is why it's often the fastest cost win available before you touch anything architectural.
